title: Legitimacy Validation through Visual Aesthetics

part_a.trigger: The system uses a semantically readable and clean URL (e.g. paypal.update-account.com) free of complex technical symbols (Visual Flaw) AND presents it while the user is focused on quickly completing a login or payment operation (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): The use of URLs such as www.paypal.hostding.com, perceived by users as clear and obvious compared to legitimate but long and complex URLs.
- Example 2 (Mobile Generalization - Revised): A system app requests the installation of a certificate named Android_Global_Trust_Fix.crt. The user trusts the familiar name without verifying its origin. The deception vector is twofold: beyond the name aesthetics, the implicit authority of the context also plays a role (the system itself is asking). The example should be understood as a variant of the base heuristic where visual trust is amplified by the perceived source. Methodological note: the error mechanism differs slightly from URL phishing as this is an active installation action, not a link click. Consider separating it into a distinct sub-example.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This triggers a distortion in Cyber Risk Beliefs. The user incorrectly believes that readability and visual order are indicators of security, while associating danger only with ugly or technical-looking interfaces.
part_a.error: The user physically clicks the action button (e.g. Login or Download) within the spoofed site instead of manually typing the official address or closing the page.
part_a.mitigation: Nudge Bundle: Ingredient 2 (Active Friction) - Insert a forced 3-second delay before allowing credential entry on infrequent external domains. Ingredient 3 (Social Cues) - Display a micro-message next to the action button: This domain has never been used by your colleagues. Verify the URL before proceeding.
part_a.criticality_context: Extremely dangerous during banking phishing attacks, corporate identity theft, or privileged account configuration.
part_a.organizational_link: Do internal policies explicitly distinguish between shortened links from approved tools (e.g. company-whitelisted shorteners) and unverified external links? Do employees know how to recognize this difference operationally?
part_a.evidence: Onarlioglu et al. (2012) demonstrate that non-technical users rely on URL length and simplicity as security cues, being deceived by readable addresses. [Onarlioglu et al., 2012 - Insights into User Behavior in Dealing with Internet Attacks]

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether the system presents links or files with clean and familiar names that conceal technical discrepancies (e.g. double extensions or malicious third-level domains). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Web: A portal displaying a link company-security.com pointing to an unverified external server. Mobile: A pop-up masking the real name of an installed package with the label Required Update.
part_b.security_risk: The interface leads the user to believe that readable equals safe. The user will click on dangerous links while ignoring technical warning signals.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle: add Active Friction (3-second delay) and Social Cues highlighting whether the domain is unknown to the organization.
part_b.org_question: Do internal policies explicitly distinguish between shortened links from approved tools (e.g. company-whitelisted shorteners) and unverified external links? Do employees know how to recognize this difference operationally?
part_b.reference: Onarlioglu et al. (2012) - Insights into User Behavior in Dealing with Internet Attacks

title: Neutralizing Visual Deception and URL Transparency

part_a.trigger: The system presents a link or call to action (CTA) that appears aesthetically 'trustworthy' because it is semantically readable (e.g., paypal.update-account.com) or that hides the actual destination through shorteners (e.g., bit.ly) or truncations in the mobile interface (Visual Flaw), AND does so while the user is under time pressure or immersed in a rapid workflow (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Semantic Phishing): The use of URLs like www.microsoft.security-login.it. The user sees familiar, 'ordered' terms, instinctively associating them with security.
- Example 2 (Mobile Truncation): A push notification from a courier with a link bit.ly/pacco-bloccato. On smartphones, the lack of a preview (hover) prevents the user from seeing that the link points to a malicious domain.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This combination triggers a double cognitive failure: 1. Distortion of Cyber Risk Beliefs (the user mistakenly believes that 'readable = safe'). 2. Attentional Tunneling (the urgency of the message narrows the user's attention, leading them to ignore domain details and focus solely on solving the immediate problem).
part_a.error: The user performs an impulsive tap or click (usually within 2-3 seconds of viewing) instead of performing a security check (e.g., long-pressing to preview or manually typing the address).
part_a.mitigation: The Behavioral Bundle: Ingredient 1 (Response-Contingent Feedback) - Upon click, a pop-up highlights the root domain in contrasting colors. Ingredient 2 (Active Friction) - Insert a forced 3-second delay or a 'slider confirmation' for links from domains outside the organization.
part_a.criticality_context: Extremely dangerous in mobile contexts (where small screens and immediate notifications reduce thinking ability), online banking, or mobile corporate credential management.
part_a.organizational_link: Do company policies prohibit the use of unapproved link shorteners? Is there monitoring of employee reaction times to critical communications to identify profiles at risk of impulsivity?
part_a.evidence: Synthesis of Onarlioglu et al. (2012) [Insights into User Behavior in Dealing with Internet Attacks] and Timko et al. (2023) [Understanding Influences on SMS Phishing Detection: User Behavior, Demographics, and Message Attributes].

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether the system features critical links or CTAs that point to external domains using familiar names or shortened/obscured formats (Visual Flaw) without providing native preemptive inspection tools or forced flow interruptions (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Web: A portal displaying the link azienda-sicurezza.com actually pointing to an unverified server. Mobile: A Delivery Notification message containing a shortened URL (bit.ly/3xYz) without any indication of the actual destination domain.
part_b.security_risk: The interface tricks the user into mistaking neat aesthetics for technical security and operational haste for necessity. This triggers quick thinking (System 1), bypassing analytical checks and resulting in the compromise of credentials.
part_b.remediation: Implement a mandatory Behavioral Bundle: 1. Active Friction (3-second timer or confirmation slider for external links). 2. URL Transparency (clear and isolated display of the root domain before the final redirect).
part_b.org_question: Does the organization conduct phishing tests that vary in visual complexity to map vulnerability to scam aesthetics? For users identified as 'serial clickers,' does the company implement additional technical barriers (e.g., isolated browsers) or simply repeat the same theoretical training course?
part_b.reference: Onarlioglu et al. (2012); Timko et al. (2023)

title: Concretizing the Abstract Threat

part_a.trigger: The system presents security warnings or backup reminders in a generic, passive, and text-only manner (Visual Flaw) AND does so while the user is immersed in their ordinary workflow (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A system message suggesting backup without showing the real impact of ransomware, leaving the risk as an abstract concept.
- Example 2 (Cloud Generalization): A corporate dashboard showing Security Status: 60% without explaining which specific files would be lost in the event of a breach.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This activates Cyber Risk Beliefs tied to unrealistic optimism (it will not happen to me). Without a tangible perception of severity, the user does not change their behavior.
part_a.error: The user physically clicks Dismiss or Remind me later to remove the interruption and return to their task.
part_a.mitigation: Nudge Bundle: Ingredient 1 (Response-Contingent Feedback - Revised) - The warning displays a blurred preview of the user personal files (e.g. photo folder or recent documents) to simulate the effect of ransomware. Important: to avoid alarm fatigue, activation must be restricted to cases where backup has been absent beyond critical thresholds (e.g. more than 7 days), and must always be paired with an immediately available action (Back up now). Ingredient 4 (Aversive Signals) - Use a high-contrast warning with loss-framing: Without a backup, you will permanently lose access to these 50 critical files.
part_a.criticality_context: Essential for ransomware prevention and data backup policy configuration.
part_a.organizational_link: Are there productivity metrics that penalize employees if they interrupt work to perform manual security procedures?
part_a.evidence: Yilmaz et al. (2023) demonstrate through qualitative interviews with ransomware victims that direct experience of the attack is the primary factor transforming risk from an abstract threat into a concrete perception, motivating lasting behavioral changes. [Yilmaz et al., 2023 - Personality Types and Ransomware Victimisation]

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether security notifications communicate the specific and tangible impact on the user data, or whether they remain in abstract technical terminology. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Enterprise: A message reading Backup not performed in 30 days appearing as a small grey icon in the system tray. Cloud: An Insecure DNS Configuration warning that does not explain the risk of personal email interception.
part_b.security_risk: The user perceives the risk as irrelevant to their personal situation. This leads to ignoring critical defenses in order to maintain operational speed.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle: use Dynamic Feedback (RCF) simulating data loss and Aversive Signals (loss-framing) to make the damage immediately understandable.
part_b.org_question: Does the organization provide post-attack psychological support to help employees manage stress and turn the incident into lasting awareness?
part_b.reference: Yilmaz et al. (2023) - Personality Types and Ransomware Victimisation

title: Prevention of Truth Bias in Familiar Interfaces

part_a.trigger: The system presents a link or a social engineering message using the exact same visual format (layout, font, colors) as legitimate messages from trusted contacts (Visual Flaw), and does so in a context of fast scrolling or habitual use of the social network (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A fake message from a friend on a social network that exploits the familiarity of the environment to make the user click on a malicious link, completely bypassing critical attention.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Enterprise): An enterprise messaging app like Teams that shows a malicious link sent by a compromised or external account with the same reassuring visual preview as verified internal links.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Truth Bias and heuristic processing. Believing in the honesty of others is a default automatic cognitive state that simplifies social interactions, leading the user to mistake threats for truth within a familiar environment.
part_a.error: The user will physically click on the link or automatically share the post without adequate cognitive processing.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a 'Behavioral Bundle' using Effort Asymmetry and Social/Rule Cues. When the user clicks on an unverified external link, the system must block the immediate redirection, inserting friction (e.g., a mandatory 3-second timer) and showing a microcopy that breaks the visual homogeneity indicating a clear rule (e.g., 'You are leaving the trusted network, verify the URL').
part_a.criticality_context: Direct messages (DMs) on social media, news feeds, internal chat systems.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization evaluate or reward response speed and 'real-time' communication, thereby reducing the time available to employees for the systematic analysis of messages?
part_a.evidence: The study confirms that the habit of reacting to social media posts leads users to apply heuristic processing, making them significantly more susceptible to phishing attacks. Individuals remain in a 'truth-default' state until the interface actively triggers suspicion through visible incongruities.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system presents an external link or a potential social engineering message using the exact same visual format (layout, font, colors) as legitimate messages from trusted contacts (Visual Flaw), and if it does so in a context of fast scrolling or habitual platform use where analytical attention is low (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Social Media): A fake message from a friend on a social network that exploits the familiarity of the environment to make the user click on a malicious link, completely bypassing critical attention. | Domain B (Enterprise): An enterprise messaging app (e.g., Slack or Teams) that shows a malicious link sent by a compromised account with the same reassuring standard visual preview used for safe links sent by colleagues.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces Truth Bias and heuristic processing of information. The user relies on the familiar environment and the 'truth-default' (automatically believing that the message is legitimate). Consequently, the user will physically click on the link or automatically share the post in less than a second, without performing a critical analysis of the source.
part_b.remediation: Implement a 'Behavioral Bundle'. When a user clicks on an unverified external link in a familiar environment, the system must block the immediate redirection (Effort Asymmetry/Friction via a mandatory 3-second timer) and show a microcopy that breaks visual homogeneity indicating a clear rule (Social/Rule Cue: 'You are leaving the trusted network, verify the URL before proceeding').
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization evaluate or reward employees for response speed and 'real-time' communication, effectively reducing the time available to them for the systematic analysis of messages?
part_b.reference: Susceptibility to phishing on social network sites: A personality information processing model

title: Prevention of Automation Bias in Complex Transactions

part_a.trigger: The interface presents a cryptographic authorization request or a transaction omitting to translate the technical data into readable language (Visual Flaw), and does so during a process driven by speculation, hype, or strict time limits (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A poorly designed and complex interface for trading NFTs that requires the user to sign a smart contract without clearly explaining which assets they are granting access to, causing fatal operational errors.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Mobile Banking): A traditional banking app that shows the terms of an international wire transfer in a dense tabular format of routing and SWIFT codes, pushing the user to blindly click the large green "Confirm" button without reading.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This triggers an Automation/Default Bias. Due to the "blockchain trust paradox" (trust is built into the technology but is not clearly experienced by the user), the user gives up in the face of complexity and blindly trusts the interface, assuming the default action is safe.
part_a.error: The user will physically approve the malicious transaction or click "Sign" in the wallet without verifying the granted permissions.
part_a.mitigation: Use Response-Contingent Feedback and Active Friction. The system must translate the technical complexity into an immediate visual summary of the consequences (e.g., "You are about to transfer ownership of X"). If the transaction deviates from the user's habitual patterns, the interface must hide the default "Confirm" button and require the user to type the exact amount or a keyword before unlocking it.
part_a.criticality_context: Approval of smart contracts, financial transactions (DeFi/NFT), installation of browser extensions with elevated privileges.
part_a.organizational_link: Is the company's design team evaluated based on metrics that favor a "frictionless" user experience to increase trading volumes, sacrificing the clarity of security information so as not to scare the user?
part_a.evidence: Research shows that complex and poorly designed NFT interfaces significantly increase user errors and susceptibility to fraud. The paradox between the secure architecture of the technology (like blockchain) and usability barriers undermines trust and leads the user to make decisions based on flawed heuristics rather than objective verification.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the interface presents an authorization request (e.g., system permissions or cryptographic transactions) omitting to translate complex technical data into a readable language (Visual Flaw), and if it does so during a process driven by strict time limits, speculation, or goal-oriented workflows (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Web3/NFT): A poorly designed interface for trading NFTs that requires the user to sign a smart contract without clearly explaining in natural language which assets they are granting access to, causing operational errors. | Domain B (Mobile Banking/Fintech): A banking app that shows the terms of an international wire transfer in a dense tabular format of incomprehensible SWIFT codes, presenting a huge green "Confirm" button that pushes the user to blindly click to overcome the obstacle.
part_b.security_risk: This interface triggers the Automation Bias (or Default Bias). Due to cognitive overload and the incomprehensibility of the technical data, the user gives up and blindly trusts the system. The user will physically approve the transaction or click on "Sign/Allow" without verifying the permissions, mistakenly assuming that the default highlighted action is safe.
part_b.remediation: Use a "Behavioral Bundle" with Response-Contingent Feedback and Active Friction. The system must translate the complexity into an immediate visual summary (e.g., icons showing what goes in and out of the wallet). If the transaction is anomalous or high-risk, the interface must remove the default "Confirm" button and require an intentional physical action from the user, such as typing the exact amount or the word "APPROVE" to unlock the operation.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Is the design/development team evaluated based on metrics that favor a "frictionless" user experience to increase operation completion volumes, sacrificing the clarity of security information?
part_b.reference: Towards More Secure Interactions: Understanding User Experience and Behaviour in the NFT Domain

title: Disruption of Deceptive Fluency in Identity Verification

part_a.trigger: The system presents a high-risk request for action (ex. a link) by perfectly mimicking the style and sender of trusted communications (Visual Flaw) AND it does so without interrupting the user's natural reading flow (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An SMS appearing in a previously legitimate conversation (with the same sender ID) that says 'Your account has been blocked, click here to unblock,' prompting the user to click on a link that redirects to a clone website.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A messaging app (such as Telegram) that allows external bots to send fake 'System Notifications' messages with the text structure, profile picture, and description consistent with the app's standard notifications.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The design exploits the lack of analytical reflection (low TRDM), and the user processes information heuristically (automatically and quickly) rather than systematically, skipping situation evaluation and analysis of alternatives.
part_a.error: The user physically clicks on the malicious link instead of ignoring the message and opening the banking app to check the account status or other reported communications.
part_a.mitigation: Implementation of an 'Active Friction' Behavioral Bundle: 1. Effort Asymmetry (e.g., a full-screen overlay with a slider to proceed) to interrupt the natural flow. 2. Social/Rule Cues (e.g., a message stating 'Security policy requires manual review for unidentified external links').
part_a.criticality_context: Financial management or accessing sensitive data from mobile devices, especially when the user is on the move or performing other activities on a small screen which reduces the ability to think.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the company assess employees' cognitive traits (such as TRDM) to personalize security training, or does it simply send generic alerts that are the same for everyone?
part_a.evidence: Kamar et al. (2023) demonstrates that TRDM moderates the effectiveness of security messages; subjects with low TRDM often ignored warnings and fell victim to SMiShing simulations.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether the system presents links or requests for critical action within messages that mimic the visual and textual identity of trusted communications without inserting physical interruptions or 'disfluency' cues.
part_b.violations: Domain A: SMS in official banking queue requesting data update via link without OS/app reporting external nature. Domain B: Admin panel with 'Password Expiration' button identical to routine notifications.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces low Cognitive Reflexivity. The user processes the threat through rapid/heuristic thinking (System 1) leading to an impulsive action that bypasses consideration of consequences.
part_b.remediation: Implement an 'Active Friction' Behavioral Bundle: 1. Introduce effort asymmetry (e.g., confirmation slider or 3-second timer). 2. Display a dynamic rule cue to force a shift to analytical thinking.
part_b.org_question: Does the company monitor whether phishing test error rates are tied to specific employee cognitive profiles (ex. impulsiveness) and adjust technical controls accordingly?
part_b.reference: Eden Kamar, C. Jordan Howell, David Maimon & Tamar Berenblum (2023). The Moderating Role of Thoughtfully Reflective Decision-Making on the Relationship between Information Security Messages and SMiShing Victimization.

title: Disruption of Deceptive Fluency in Identity Verification

part_a.trigger: The paper explains that SMiShing attacks are successful because the messages appear to come from apparent legitimate sources (such as the Bank of Israel, for example). If the interface used is too seamless, the targeted user doesn't activate analytical thinking. The trigger, therefore, identifies the lack of friction that allows those with “low Thoughtfully Reflective Decision Making” (TRDM) to click impulsively. Used formula: “The system presents a high-risk request for action (ex. a link) by perfectly mimicking the style and sender of trusted communications (Visual Flaw) AND it does so without interrupting the user's natural reading flow (Timing/Context Flaw).”
part_a.examples:
- Example in the paper: An SMS appearing in a previously legitimate conversation (with the same sender ID) that says something like "Your account has been blocked, click here to unblock," inviting the user to click on a link that redirects to a clone website identical to the original bank's website.
- Generalized example: A messaging app (such as Telegram) that allows external bots to send fake "System Notifications" messages with the text structure, profile picture, and description consistent with the app's standard notifications.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The paper defines TRDM (Thoughtfully Reflective Decision-Making) as a process consisting of four phases: 1. situation evaluation, 2. analysis of alternatives, 3. actual choice, 4. evaluation of results. A person with low reflectiveness skips the first two phases if the interface doesn't force them to stop with any type of warning. The design exploits the lack of analytical reflection, and the user processes information heuristically (automatically and quickly) rather than systematically.
part_a.error: The user physically clicks on the malicious link instead of ignoring the message and opening the banking app to check the account status or other reported communications.
part_a.mitigation: The paper demonstrates that simple warning messages (static text) do not work for those with low TRDM. Therefore, a physical "nudge" (a slider) is needed to interrupt the natural flow of operations and force the end user to reflect (Behavioral Bundle). Ingredient 2: (Effort Asymmetry): When the user clicks on a link from an unsaved sender, a full-screen overlay appears requiring the user to slide a slider (friction) to proceed. Ingredient 3: (Social/Rule Cues): Next to the slider, there should be a message stating, "Security policy requires manual review for unidentified external links."
part_a.criticality_context: The paper focuses on smartphone banking SMiShing, saying that the mobile context (the smartphone) is a critical factor, as the small screen and rapid notifications further reduce the user's ability to think. Dangerous situations could be related to financial management or accessing sensitive data from mobile devices, especially when the user is on the move or is already performing another activity.
part_a.organizational_link: The paper concludes by stating that one size does not fit all, meaning that security alerts work for thoughtful employees but are useless for impulsive ones. The organization's role must therefore be to address the issue of how to protect this most vulnerable group of users. The question the inspector should ask company management is: "Does the company consider employees' cognitive traits (such as TRDM) when implementing its safety training program? Or does it focus on more technical aspects?"
part_a.evidence: The study by Kamar et al. (2023) demonstrates that "Thoughtfully Reflective Decision-Making" (TRDM) moderates the effectiveness of security messages. Specifically, most subjects with low TRDM ignored security warnings and fell victim to the SMiShing simulation, regardless of their level of preparedness. The paper provides statistical data that scientifically confirms that behavior (the user's tapping on the link) is directly influenced by the cognitive trait of reflexivity.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether the system presents links or requests for critical action within messages that mimic the visual and textual identity of trusted communications (Visual Flaw) without inserting physical interruptions or "disfluency" cues that force the user out of automatic response mode (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_b.violations: Domain A (Mobile/SMS - From the paper): An SMS received in an official banking message queue that requests an immediate "data update" via a clickable link, without the operating system or messaging app reporting the external/unverified nature of the link. Domain B (Enterprise Dashboard - Generalization): An admin panel that displays a "Password Expiration" notification with a "Reset Now" button identical in style and placement to a routine notification, prompting the user to click without checking the destination URL.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces low Cognitive Reflexivity (Low TRDM). The user processes the threat through rapid/heuristic thinking (System 1) rather than analytical thinking (System 2). The result is an impulsive action (clicking on the link) that bypasses consideration of the consequences, leading to victimization by SMS or phishing.
part_b.remediation: Implement an "Active Friction" Behavioral Bundle. When the user attempts to click on a high-risk link, the system should: 1. Introduce an effort asymmetry (ex. a confirmation slider or a 3-second timer before the link opens) and 2. Display a dynamic rule cue ("Company policy requires manual verification for external banking links") to force the user to shift to analytical thinking.
part_b.org_question: When interviewing managers, ask: "Does the company assess whether phishing test failure rates correlate with specific employee cognitive profiles (ex. impulsiveness)? Does it analyze the resulting data to implement specific controls or develop specific training programs (ex. employee reprimands)?"
part_b.reference: Eden Kamar, C. Jordan Howell, David Maimon & Tamar Berenblum. The Moderating Role of Thoughtfully Reflective Decision-Making on the Relationship between Information Security Messages and SMiShing Victimization: An Experiment.

title: Disruption of Attentional Tunneling in Mobile Messaging

part_a.trigger: The system presents a notification or message containing a shortened or obscured URL, giving maximum visual emphasis to the 'Urgency' element (ex. 'Action required now!') (Visual Flaw) AND it does so without providing any native tool for safely previewing the link before physical interaction (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An SMS from a delivery service (ex. USPS) reporting a 'held package' with a 'bit.ly link' or a misspelled URL (ex. post-it-delivery.com) that the user overlooks due to focus on the package issue.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A notification from a financial app stating 'Unauthorized access! Click here' where the mobile interface truncates the real address, preventing the user from seeing that the domain is not the official one.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The interface creates an 'attention tunnel' on the action (the click) rather than on reflection. Users with low attention spans or under superficial processing fail to analyze 'Message Attributes' (URL structure, sender) because technical details are hidden to maintain a cleaner UI.
part_a.error: The user will physically tap the link quickly within the first 2 seconds, instead of performing any safe inspection action (ex. long press to preview the full URL).
part_a.mitigation: Behavioral Bundle to force attention: 1. Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF): A pop-up highlighting the root domain in bold red requiring the user to enter the first three letters of the site to proceed. 2. Effort Asymmetry: Disabling direct clicks from unknown senders, forcing a 2-second long-press to activate the link.
part_a.criticality_context: Managing credentials, security updates, or tracking shipments in mobile multitasking environments where attention is divided, encouraging user impulsivity.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization measure how much time employees spend reading safety communications or only assess whether they have 'completed' the training module?
part_a.evidence: Timko et al. (2023) found that attention is the most significant predictor of smishing detection accuracy; participants who analyzed message details (URL, grammar) had significantly higher success rates.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether the system presents links or CTAs using shortened, obscured, or truncated URLs, visually prioritizing urgency without providing a built-in inspection or mandatory link preview before opening.
part_b.violations: Domain A: Delivery notification containing 'bit.ly/3xYz' without destination domain info. Domain B: Push notification displaying only 'Tap to secure your account', completely hiding the target web address.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces a decline in Cognitive Reflexivity focused on Attention. The user's focus is directed exclusively to emotional content (urgency), leading to impulsive tapping that bypasses security knowledge.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle: 1. Effort Asymmetry (require long press to activate link). 2. Response-Contingent Feedback (clear preview of the root domain in contrasting color with explicit confirmation required).
part_b.org_question: Does the organization conduct phishing tests that vary based on message complexity (ex. shortened vs. long URLs) to identify susceptibility to attentional tunneling under pressure?
part_b.reference: Daniel Timko, Daniel Hernandez Castillo, Muhammad Lutfor Rahman. Understanding Influences on SMS Phishing Detection: User Behavior, Demographics, and Message Attributes.

part_b.remediation: Implement a mandatory Behavioral Bundle: 1. Active Friction (3-second timer or confirmation slider for external links). 2. URL Transparency (clear and isolated display of the root domain before the final redirect).
part_b.org_question: Does the organization conduct phishing tests that vary in visual complexity to map vulnerability to scam aesthetics? For users identified as 'serial clickers,' does the company implement additional technical barriers (e.g., isolated browsers) or simply repeat the same theoretical training course?
part_b.reference: Onarlioglu et al. (2012); Timko et al. (2023)

title: Workload-Agnostic Security Design and Phishing Susceptibility

part_a.trigger: The system presents security warnings or administrative notifications using a static visual design AND it fails to adapt the delivery, timing, or prominence of these alerts based on the user's real-time workload intensity or documented peak operational windows
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Directly from Literature - Paper 1): Hospital staff receiving "announcements and other general notes" via email while simultaneously managing heavy patient loads or clinical emergencies. Because the system does not prioritize or delay these messages during peak times, overworked staff process them on "autopilot".
- Example 2 (Generalization): A corporate mobile app pushes a high-priority "Security Policy Update" alert using the same standard white pop-up used for benign social notifications while the user is in a high-stress environment (e.g., a busy commute), leading to a reflexive click just to clear the screen
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design actively induces Cognitive Fatigue (HF in the MORPHEUS model). This is a state of reduced mental capacity that occurs following prolonged engagement in cognitively demanding tasks. By remaining static and passive in the face of an overloaded user, the interface allows the brain to remain in an automatic and distorted "System 1" state, preventing the necessary transition to the deliberate and analytical thinking of "System 2."
part_a.error: The user will physically click on a malicious phishing link in less than 2 seconds (a reflexive action to "clear" the interface task) instead of performing a deliberate inspection of the sender's identity or the destination URL.
part_a.mitigation:
- • Ingredient 1: Effort Asymmetry (Active Friction). The system will implement a 3-second non-clickable delay on external links during peak workload hours to disrupt the automatic click loop
- • Ingredient 3 (Rule Cues): Display a clear behavioral prompt: "High Workload Detected: Avoid clicking links now. Use the 'Remind me in 1 hour' button to review this safely later."
part_a.criticality_context: Most dangerous in emergency healthcare settings, cyber incident response centers, or during high-stakes financial auditing.
part_a.organizational_link: 1. "Does the organization have a formal policy to limit 'extensive emailing' (e.g., non-urgent announcements, general notes) to reduce the daily cognitive load on clinical staff?".
part_a.evidence: Jalali et al. (2020) demonstrated that workload was the only variable significantly associated with actual clicking behavior on phishing links, proving that high cognitive load makes staff too occupied to notice imposed threats

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system presents security warnings or administrative notifications using a static visual design AND fails to adapt the delivery, timing, or prominence of these alerts based on the user's real-time workload intensity or documented peak operational windows. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Healthcare - Literature): Clinical staff receive a high volume of non-urgent administrative emails (e.g., general announcements) in the same format as critical alerts while simultaneously managing emergency patient intakes or heavy patient loads.
- Domain B (Corporate Mobile): A high-priority "Security Policy Update" alert is delivered via a standard white pop-up (identical to low-risk social notifications) while the user is in a high-stress environment, such as a busy commute.
part_b.security_risk: This design actively induces Cognitive Fatigue (Cognitive HF in the MORPHEUS model). Prolonged engagement in demanding tasks depletes mental resources, forcing the user into an automatic, distorted "System 1" state. As a result, the user will physically click on a malicious phishing link in less than 2 seconds, just to eliminate the distraction and return to their primary work.
part_b.remediation: 1. Active Friction Implement a 3-second non-clickable delay on external links during peak workload hours to disrupt the automatic click loop. 2. Rule Cues: Display a dynamic prompt stating: "High Workload Detected: Avoid clicking links now. Use the 'Remind me in 1 hour' button to review this safely later.
part_b.org_question: 1. "Does the organization have a formal policy to limit 'extensive emailing' (e.g., non-urgent announcements) to reduce the daily cognitive load on staff?"

title: Information-Siloed Security Reporting and Mitigation Failure

part_a.trigger: The system provides a flat, technical list of security vulnerabilities or error codes (Visual Flaw) AND it fails to provide immediate, contextualized actionable steps or copy-pasteable code snippets for remediation within the same report (Timing/Context Flaw)
part_a.examples:
- • Example 1 (Directly from Literature): A TLS scanner (like testssl.sh) that reports a server is "VULNERABLE" to CRIME or BREACH but does not explain that the fix involves disabling DEFLATE in specific Apache configuration files, forcing the admin to search external sources.
- • Example 2 (Generalization - Cloud/Enterprise): A Cloud Security dashboard flags a "Publicly Accessible Storage Bucket" but requires the administrator to navigate multiple sub-menus and external documentation to find the specific CLI command needed to restrict access.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Cognitive Fatigue (Cognitive HF in MORPHEUS; a state of diminished mental capability resulting from prolonged engagement with demanding tasks). By forcing the professional to independently research, interpret technical jargon, and synthesize information from multiple external sources under time pressure, the Ul exhausts executive functions. This mental overload leads to a reliance on "System 1" automatic processing, resulting in concentration loss and suboptimal choices.
part_a.error: The user will physically leave a dangerous configuration active or apply a partial/incorrect patch (an omission or suboptimal choice) instead of implementing the full, correct security measure.
part_a.mitigation:
- • Ingredient 1: Rule Cues. The interface must provide "Actionable Mitigations": natural language explanations of the threat paired with ready-to-use code snippets and specific file path instructions directly next to the vulnerability.
- • Ingredient 2: Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF). The report should include a "Simulated Outcome" or preview button that allows the user to see the expected change in the security report (e.g., the "Vulnerable" status turning to "Safe") before they physically apply the configuration change.
part_a.criticality_context: High-stakes infrastructure tasks, such as patching cryptographic protocols (TLS), configuring network firewalls, or managing cloud access policies.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization provide standardized, pre-verified 'Remediation Playbooks' for common vulnerabilities, or are staff expected to independently research and define mitigation strategies while managing high daily workloads?.
part_a.evidence: Manfredi et al. (2021) experimentally proved that reports with actionable hints reduce the time to fix vulnerabilities by 3 times and increase patch correctness from 67% to 98%

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if security vulnerability reports provide a flat list of technical defects without including immediate actionable mitigations, such as contextual explanations or ready-to-use code snippets. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (TLS Scanners): A report indicates a "CRIME" vulnerability but does not provide the specific Apache configuration lines required to disable TLS compression.
- Domain B (Cloud Admin): An enterprise dashboard flags a misconfigured firewall rule but requires the user to leave the interface to find the vendor-specific documentation for the fix.
part_b.security_risk: SECURITY RISK (Risk Profile): This interface induces Cognitive Fatigue. By forcing users to perform independent research and synthesize complex data from external sources, the Ul exhausts mental resources. Fatigued admins switch to "System 1" thinking and will leave configurations insecure or apply incorrect patches due to concentration loss and suboptimal decision-making.
part_b.remediation: 1_rule_cues : Embed natural language explanations and copy-pasteable code snippets directly within the vulnerability report. 2_rcf: Response-Contingent Feedback: Provide a "Dry-Run" preview that shows the user how the security status will change after the patch is applied.
part_b.org_question: ORGANIZATIONAL AUDIT QUESTION (Audit Context): "Does the company rely on employees' individual research to solve technical vulnerabilities, thereby ignoring the cognitive fatigue caused by information-gathering under pressure?"
part_b.reference: Evidence: Manfredi et al. (2021). Do Security Reports Meet Usability? Lessons Learned from Using Actionable Mitigations..

title: Analyzing Cybercrime Victimization: The Roles of Online Frequency, Tasks, and Information Posting

part_a.trigger: The system places high-risk transactional modules between (online banking, e-commerce checkout) and direct communication channels (email client, notification inbox) within the same interface session, accessible via a single click or tab switch, with no visual, temporal, or procedural boundary separating them (Visual/Structural Flaw). Furthermore, the system delivers incoming email notifications or message previews passively in a sidebar or status bar while the user is actively completing a financial transaction, pulling their attention toward communication content before the secure task is finished (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): The authors of [1] found that users who conduct online banking AND read news AND shop online show significantly elevated phishing victimization rates, each independently. This is not coincidental overlap — these are activities that prime users to expect legitimate-looking institutional messages. A unified browser session where a user completes a bank transfer, reads a financial news article, and then opens their email inbox in the same tab group has no mechanism to signal that their threat context has changed. The phishing email that arrives framed as a 'transaction confirmation' lands in exactly the mental environment the attacker designed it for.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A corporate ERP platform (SAP, Oracle, similar) where employees process purchase orders or approve budget transfers through a finance module, and the same platform embeds an internal notification feed showing messages from colleagues and external vendors. An attacker who has compromised a vendor email account sends a spoofed 'invoice update' message through the vendor communication channel. The employee, still mentally inside a financial approval workflow, physically clicks the link without switching to a verification mindset because the interface never signaled that they left the secure transaction context.
- Example 3 (Generalization): A banking app that, upon completing a transfer, immediately surfaces a 'You might also like' panel showing promotional offers with embedded links, or worse, redirects the user to a partner retail site within the same app session. The user's mental frame is still 'I just did something financial and legitimate here' — making them disproportionately likely to treat the next link they see as trustworthy.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This trigger directly activates the Internet Usage human factor as defined in the MORPHEUS framework. MORPHEUS defines Internet Usage as the amount of time an individual spends engaging with online environments and digital services, noting that higher usage increases exposure to potential cyber threats and reinforces habitual message processing, thereby expanding the opportunity for deceptive contact unless counterbalanced by strong awareness and self-regulatory controls. The core interface flaw driving this vulnerability is the lack of a contextual reset between completing a transaction and accessing a communication channel, which eliminates the crucial structural opportunity to interrupt a user's automatic cognitive processing. By removing these architectural boundaries, systems strip away necessary self-regulatory controls, forcing users to rely entirely on their own awareness to evaluate threats.
part_a.error: The user will physically click a URL embedded in an email or in-platform notification within the same session as completing a financial transaction, and will enter their credentials or payment information on the destination page, instead of closing the session, opening a fresh browser window, and navigating directly to the institution's known URL.
part_a.mitigation: To mitigate or prevent phishing without destroying user productivity, systems should use a mandatory transition screen immediately after a user completes a financially sensitive action. Instead of generic warnings that users quickly ignore, this screen should briefly lock the interface and display a dynamically generated message specific to the exact transaction just finished, paired with a reference to security policy. This interrupts the user's cognitive autopilot and provides a clear rule, helping them understand that the safe transaction is over and they should be on guard. However, to make this practical and avoid frustrating high-volume workers who process hundreds of tasks daily, this system must use 'adaptive friction.' Rather than forcing a strict five-second delay on every single action, the system should scale the friction based on risk. For example, it could apply the full delay to high-risk events like first-time vendor payments or large transfers, while reducing the delay for routine, repetitive approvals, ensuring the security measure remains both effective and realistic for daily business operations.
part_a.criticality_context: This flaw is most dangerous in operational sequences where a financially sensitive task completion is immediately followed by access to a communication channel within the same session. The highest-risk scenarios include completing a wire transfer or bill payment and then opening an email inbox, approving a vendor invoice in an ERP system and then reading a notification from that same vendor, completing an e-commerce checkout and then reading a delivery confirmation email in the same browser session, and logging into a corporate financial dashboard and then opening an embedded messaging tool. The common thread across all these scenarios is that the communication content the user encounters is contextually indistinguishable from legitimate institutional follow-up
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization measure employee task throughput or session efficiency in ways that would make a 5-second mandatory transition screen feel like a productivity penalty? Specifically, are financial approval workflows subject to SLA timers or volume-based performance metrics that create pressure to process transactions as fast as possible? If yes, the friction introduced by this mitigation will face internal resistance and may be quietly disabled by IT teams under pressure from operations managers, in this case policies must be introduced.
part_a.evidence: The paper [1] demonstrated through logistic regression on a sample of 277 participants that online banking and online shopping each independently increased phishing victimization odds by over 110%, while reading news online also predicted phishing victimization significantly. These effects held after controlling for demographic variables including age, employment, and education. The study operationalized these findings within the integrated lifestyle-routine activities theoretical framework, establishing that it is not general time online but specific activity combinations that create victimization risk — precisely the condition this heuristic targets at the interface design level.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify whether the system places transactional modules (banking, checkout, invoice approval, travel booking) and communication channels (email client, notification inbox, internal messaging) within the same interface session, accessible via a single click or tab switch, with no visual, temporal, or procedural boundary separating them. Furthermore, verify whether the system delivers incoming notifications or message previews passively (sidebar, status bar, badge counter) while the user is actively completing a financial transaction.
part_b.violations:
- Domain A(Consumer Banking Web Platform): A retail banking portal where the user completes a wire transfer and, without any transition screen or session break, clicks directly to an embedded inbox showing 'messages from your bank.' A phishing email framed as a transfer confirmation lands here. The interface has provided no signal that the user has left a secure transaction context and entered an unverified communication channel. The user's mental frame is still thinking he/she is doing banking, making the fraudulent message feel architecturally legitimate.
- Domain B(Enterprise ERP / Finance Module): A corporate ERP system (SAP, Oracle, or equivalent) where an employee approves vendor invoices through a finance workflow module. A notification badge from the integrated vendor messaging channel is visible in the top navigation bar throughout the approval process. Upon completing the approval, the employee clicks the badge and reads a message — which may be a spoofed vendor communication containing a fraudulent payment link. The system never signaled that moving from the approval workflow to the vendor message channel required a different threat posture.
- Domain C(Mobile Banking Application): A banking app that, immediately after a completed transfer, surfaces a promotional panel or redirects the user to a partner retail interface within the same authenticated session. No session closure, no context marker, no re-entry friction. The user remains in a high-trust mental state established by the banking interaction and treats the next interface element regardless of its actual origin with the same legitimacy they granted the bank.
part_b.security_risk: This interface activates the Internet Usage human factor as defined in the MORPHEUS framework. Higher Internet usage reinforces habitual message processing, and when a user completes a financial transaction and immediately enters a communication channel within the same session, they extend the trust frame of the transactional activity to whatever they encounter next without performing a fresh threat assessment. This is not a theoretical risk. The paper [1] demonstrated empirically that online banking and online shopping each independently elevated phishing victimization odds by over 110% after controlling for demographics. The interface design described above is the architectural condition that converts that statistical vulnerability into a live, exploitable attack surface.
part_b.remediation: Instruct the development team to add a transition screen that appears immediately after a user finishes a financial task, like a payment or money transfer the interface should use 'adaptive friction,' meaning the length of the delay adapts to the risk level of the task. For example, high-risk actions, like paying a new vendor, should trigger a full-screen lock for a few seconds, while low-risk, routine actions should trigger a much shorter delay so employees can maintain their work speed. During this brief lock, the screen must show a specific warning about the exact task the user just finished, such as, 'You just approved a payment; a real vendor will never email you a link to confirm this.' These specific messages force the user's brain to pay attention, whereas people quickly learn to ignore generic, repetitive warnings. Below the message, the screen should include a direct link to the company's security rules. Giving users a clear rule helps them understand why they have to wait, giving them a clear rule trains them to build safe, secure habits.
part_b.org_question: Are financial approval workflows or transaction processing tasks subject to throughput metrics, SLA timers, or volume-based performance targets that create measurable time pressure on employees completing these tasks? Who holds the authority to disable or shorten the mandatory session transition screen, and is that decision subject to security team review or can it be overridden unilaterally by operations or IT management under productivity pressure?
part_b.reference: Ngo, F. T. (2020). Victimization in Cyberspace: Is It How Long We Spend Online, What We Do Online, or What We Post Online? Criminal Justice Review, 430-451.

title: Individual Differences in Cybersecurity Behaviours: Analysis of Common Human Error

part_a.trigger: The system requires a multi-step, multi-screen formal process to grant temporary or delegated access to another user, while providing no visible, single-action alternative within the primary interface AND presents this delegation process exclusively through administrative or IT-mediated channels that are architecturally separated from the workflow where the sharing need actually arises, ensuring the user encounters the secure option only after they have already left the task context where the decision was made (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): The paper [1] found that lack of perseverance was the sole impulsivity subscale significantly predicting password sharing, and proposed that the mechanism is task delegation,low-perseverance users share credentials specifically to offload tasks they find tedious or effortful. The authors also found that self-monitoring was the strongest overall predictor, with high self-monitors sharing under social pressure from colleagues.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A hospital using an Electronic Medical Records system where a surgeon needs a covering colleague to access their patient files during an emergency procedure. The formal access delegation process requires contacting the system administrator, submitting a temporary privilege escalation form through the IT helpdesk portal, a separate system entirely, and waiting for manual approval. Under emergency conditions, this process is operationally impossible.
- Example 3 (Generalization): A project management platform, where a team member going on parental leave needs a colleague to manage their assigned tasks and communicate with external clients through their account. The platform offers full account transfer, permanent role reassignment, or IT-mediated permission changes all processes requiring either permanent structural changes to the account or multi-day administrative procedures.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This situation perfectly describes the 'Laziness' human factor in the MORPHEUS framework, which happens when people avoid putting in effort even when they are perfectly capable of doing a task. When it comes to sharing passwords, this laziness shows up in three main ways. First, people share their logins simply to avoid doing tedious tasks themselves. Second, the 'safe' way to grant someone access, like navigating confusing admin menus or waiting for IT approval is boring, difficult, and frustrating, so people lose interest in doing it the right way. Third, when coworkers pressure them for access, users often feel they have no quick, secure alternative, making them feel like they have no other choice. Ultimately, even people who know the security rules will still share their passwords because the system makes the unsafe choice much easier than the safe one.
part_a.error: The user will physically type their account password into a direct message, email, or verbal communication and transmit it to a colleague within the same session where the sharing need arose, instead of navigating to the platform's access delegation feature and completing the temporary access grant process, because the delegation feature is either inaccessible from the current task view or requires more sustained navigational effort than the user is willing to expend at that moment.
part_a.mitigation: Instruct the development team to implement a 'Secure Delegation Feature' directly within the primary task interface. A permanently visible 'Share Access' button should open a simple two-field overlay: select a colleague and set an expiry date. The system then automatically provisions and revokes access without further administrative burden. If an atypical or concurrent login is detected, this same overlay must automatically interrupt the active session to prompt secure delegation. Adjacent to the confirmation, include a policy anchor. This removes user fears regarding future administrative effort or loss of control. The underlying, non-negotiable design principle is simple: the secure path must be faster than insecurely sharing a password.
part_a.criticality_context: This flaw is most dangerous in environments where temporary access delegation is a routine operational need rather than an exceptional event. Financial approval workflows represent the highest risk, since shared credentials in this context create unauditable transactions where payment authorization and budget transfers cannot be traced to a single accountable individual. Healthcare records systems carry equivalent severity, where temporary clinical access is needed routinely across shifts and between covering physicians, and shared credentials violate patient data protection regulations independently of whether any data is actually misused. Enterprise email systems present a consistently high-risk condition because inbox delegation is a standard operational need for executives and their assistants, and shared credentials in this context expose the organization's entire communication history to anyone who subsequently compromises the delegate's device. Across all these environments the common thread is predictability, these are not exceptional edge cases but recurring operational scenarios that the interface has failed to accommodate securely.
part_a.organizational_link: Is the IT helpdesk team measured on ticket volume, ticket resolution time, or other throughput metrics that would be negatively affected by reducing the complexity of the access delegation process? If so, who has the authority to redesign the delegation workflow, and does that authority sit with the security team or with IT operations?. Has the organization measured or observed how frequently employees share credentials during high-pressure operational periods and has credential sharing during these periods been formally addressed in policy, or has it been informally tolerated as an operational necessity?
part_a.evidence: The authors of the paper [1] demonstrated that lack of perseverance or laziness significantly predicted password sharing (B=0.05, Wald=4.29, p=0.04) while cyber security knowledge did not (p=0.08). Self-monitoring was the strongest predictor overall (B=0.07, Wald=9.64, p<0.001). The model correctly classified 62.6% of cases. The specific theoretical implication drawn by the authors, that low-perseverance users share passwords to delegate effortful tasks to others, provides the direct behavioral mechanism this heuristic targets at the interface design level.

part_b.audit_rule: From the primary task interface, the inbox view, the task board, the financial approval screen, the patient record view, attempt to grant a colleague temporary access to your account without navigating away from your current screen. You are looking for two things simultaneously: whether a delegation or temporary access feature is visible and reachable from this exact view, and if it is, whether completing it requires more than three clicks or involves navigating to a separate administrative system, submitting a helpdesk ticket, or waiting for IT approval. If the feature is absent from the primary task view entirely, or if it exists but demands navigational effort incompatible with the operational reality of a user under time pressure, this rule is violated. A delegation feature buried in administrative settings that the average user has never visited is behaviorally equivalent to no delegation feature at all, invisibility and inaccessibility produce the same outcome: the user shares their password instead.
part_b.violations:
- Domain A(Enterprise Email): A corporate email client where inbox delegation exists as a feature but is accessible only through the account settings panel, requiring the user to exit their inbox, navigate through three or more settings subcategories, and enter the delegate's address in a configuration form. No delegation prompt appears when the user attempts to forward their credentials or when a concurrent session is detected. The primary inbox view contains no visible delegation affordance. A user going on leave who needs an assistant to manage their correspondence will share their password in a Teams message rather than locate and complete this process under time pressure.
- Domain B(Healthcare EHR System):A clinical records platform where temporary access delegation for covering physicians requires submission of a helpdesk ticket through a separate IT portal, with manual approval from the system administrator. No temporary access option exists within the patient record view or the clinical dashboard. Under shift-handover or emergency conditions, the formal process is operationally incompatible with the time available. Credentials are shared verbally or via clinical messaging. This violation carries regulatory consequences under patient data protection law that extend beyond the individual security incident.
- Domain C(Project Management SaaS): A task management platform where the only mechanisms for giving a colleague access to an account are full ownership transfer or IT-mediated role escalation, both permanent or semi-permanent changes requiring administrative intervention. No ‘temporary delegate’ or ‘grant access until date’ feature exists in the standard user interface. An employee preparing for parental leave shares their login credentials with a colleague via direct message because the platform offers no operationally viable alternative within the time and effort constraints of their departure preparation.
part_b.security_risk: This interface activates the Laziness human factor as defined in the MORPHEUS framework, an aversion to effortful activity despite having the capacity to perform it. When the secure delegation path requires more sustained navigational effort than sharing a password verbally or via message, the system has made the insecure behavior the path of least resistance, critically, cybersecurity knowledge did not distinguish sharers from non-sharers in that study — meaning users sharing credentials in this system are not unaware that it is inadvisable. They share because the interface architecture left them no easier alternative at the moment the decision was made.
part_b.remediation: Instruct the development team to implement a Secure Delegation Feature built directly into the primary task interface ,not in settings, not through IT mediation, but on the same screen where work is performed. The feature works as follows: at the exact view where a user would logically need to share access, a clearly labeled ‘Share Access’ button is permanently visible. Clicking it opens a two-field overlay: select a colleague from the organizational directory, set an expiry date. One confirmation tap provisions access automatically, notifies the delegate immediately, and schedules automatic revocation at the chosen time with no further action required from anyone. If the system detects a concurrent login from an unfamiliar device or location, this same overlay surfaces automatically as a non-dismissable prompt in the active session, offering the secure delegation path at the exact moment sharing is likely occurring.
part_b.org_question: Is the IT helpdesk team measured on ticket volume or resolution throughput in ways that would be negatively affected by simplifying the access delegation process? Who holds the authority to redesign the delegation workflow? Is it documented? Has the organization observed or formally acknowledged that credential sharing occurs during high-pressure operational periods such as shift handovers, employee leave, or deadline periods? If so, has this been addressed in written policy, or has it been informally tolerated as an operational necessity by line managers?
part_b.reference: Whitty, M. D. (2015). Individual differences in cyber security behaviors: an examination of who is sharing passwords. Cyberpsychology, behavior and social networking, 3–7.

title: Procedural Awareness Integration in Threat Validation

part_a.trigger: The system issues a high-level security warning (e.g., 'Suspicious Link Detected') providing only conceptual information about the risk (Visual Flaw) AND it fails to provide an immediate, 'in-place' mechanism for the user to perform a validation check before the final choice is made (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An anti-phishing tool that marks an email as 'Suspicious' but does not offer a way to safely inspect the destination URL. The user is aware it might be phishing but lacks the procedure to verify it.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A mobile app requesting 'Accessibility Permissions' with a generic warning. The system provides no interactive guide or specific examples of what data the app will read, leaving the user with a 'conceptual' fear but no 'procedural' way to audit the app's intent.
part_a.human_factor_exp: According to Asanka & Love, conceptual knowledge alone does not increase self-efficacy; users need to know 'how' to perform the avoidance behavior.
part_a.error: The user will physically click 'Accept/Proceed anyway' within seconds because they lack the practical tools to validate the threat, leading to a 'forced' bypass of the security prompt.
part_a.mitigation: Implement Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF) and Social/Rule Cues. The interface must require the user to perform a 'Verification Ritual' (e.g., hover over a link for 2 seconds to reveal its true source). The 'Proceed' button remains locked until this RCF is triggered. Alongside, a Rule Cue should state: 'Company Policy 4.2 requires manual URL verification to prevent credential theft.'
part_a.criticality_context: Phishing detection, granting high-level OS permissions.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization’s security training focus only on 'spotting the signs' (conceptual) or does it provide tools and time for 'verification steps' (procedural) during the workday?
part_a.evidence: Asanka & Love (2014)

part_b.audit_rule: Integrate Procedural Awareness > Inspection Check: Verify if the system, when flagging a threat, provides only a text warning or if it provides a functional 'check-step' (e.g., an inspection tool) that allows the user to verify the threat before deciding.
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Email): A mail client warns 'External Sender' but provides no safe way to preview attachment metadata or link targets without opening them.
- Domain B (Mobile): An OS-level prompt asks for 'Full Disk Access' but does not show a 'View what this app will see' button, leaving the user procedurally blind.
part_b.security_risk: Lack of Procedural Awareness. The user knows there is a risk but doesn't know how to handle it, leading them to ignore the warning to finish their task.
part_b.remediation: Implement a 'Verification Bundle.' Use Active Friction (locking the 'Accept' button) until a Response-Contingent Feedback (e.g., a 2-second hover or a manual expansion of the URL) is completed. Pair this with a Rule Cue explaining the specific policy.
part_b.org_question: Does management penalize employees for the extra time spent using security verification tools?
part_b.reference: Asanka & Love (2014)

title: Explicit Impact Mapping for Security Misconfigurations

part_a.trigger: The system allows the user to change a security-critical setting in an isolated text-field or toggle (Visual Flaw) AND it does not dynamically visualize the resulting change in the overall 'attack surface' or compliance status at the moment of the change (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A Cloud dashboard where a user modifies a WAF rule. The system allows the change without alerting the user that this specific rule permits access to the Metadata Service.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A network admin tool where opening a port is treated as a simple 'on/off' switch without showing a map of which internal assets become visible to the public internet.
part_a.human_factor_exp: Users lack the 'Big Picture' of how a single technical change creates a 'Deadly Threat' as defined by Gupta et al.
part_a.error: The user will physically click 'Apply Changes' to fix a connectivity issue, unknowingly creating a massive security breach (e.g., making a private database public).
part_a.mitigation: Implement Effort Asymmetry (Friction) and Aversive Signals. For high-impact changes, the system must trigger a 'Consequence Modal' using high-contrast loss-framing (e.g., 'This change exposes 5 sensitive servers'). The user must wait for a 3-second countdown (Friction) before they can type 'I UNDERSTAND' to confirm the action.
part_a.criticality_context: Cloud Resource Management, Firewall Configuration, Identity & Access Management.
part_a.organizational_link: Is there a 'Fast-Fix' culture that encourages admins to bypass security checks to minimize downtime?
part_a.evidence: Gupta et al. (2023)

part_b.audit_rule: Enforce Impact Awareness > Inspection Check: Verify if the interface dynamically shows the 'Security Impact' (e.g., exposed assets) during the configuration process or if it treats critical changes as simple, isolated toggles. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Cloud): An S3 bucket settings page that allows 'Public Read Access' without displaying a high-contrast warning of exactly which files will be indexed by search engines.
- Domain B (IoT): A smart-device dashboard that allows disabling 'Secure Boot' with a single click, without explaining that this allows unsigned malicious firmware to run.
part_b.security_risk: Misconfiguration via Lack of Awareness. The user lacks the mental model to understand that a small UI change has a catastrophic security consequence.
part_b.remediation: Implement 'Impact-Friction'. When a high-risk toggle is flipped, present an Aversive Signal (red high-contrast warning) and require a 3-second 'cooling-off' period before the 'Apply' button becomes active.
part_b.org_question: Are administrators required to document the 'why' of a security change in a way that forces them to consider the risks?
part_b.reference: Gupta et al. (2023)

title: Compulsive Click Behavior Prevention by Active Friction

part_a.trigger: The system presents alarms or notifications with high anxiety/emergencies containing interactive visual elements for immediate resolution (Visual Flaw) AND allows them to be executed instantly and without friction (e.g. a clickable link or a direct button) right at the moment of maximum stress or uncertainty for the user (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From the literature): A pandemic-themed phishing email that warns of "COVID-19 cases on the rise in your area" by presenting a large blue clickable "SEE NEW CASES IN YOUR AREA" button.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Banking Mobile App): A push notification on the phone that reads "Suspicious activity detected on the card" followed by a single direct "Verify Now" button that opens an external web page, without requiring prior login in the secure app.
- Example 3 (Generalization - Enterprise): A fake corporate IT alert that communicates "Account deactivation imminent" and includes a direct link to confirm credentials, taking advantage of the urgency of not losing access to work.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design activates Compulsive Behavior (specifically, compulsive checking and reassurance seeking). When faced with an ambiguous threat, the user experiences psychological distress and an uncontrollable urge to regain control of the situation. The presence of an immediate link offers a false and fast way to obtain the reassurance sought.
part_a.error: The user performs the physical action of clicking on the link or opening the attachment instantly (in less than 1 second) in an attempt to find reassurances or details, instead of performing the safe action of manually opening the official portal by typing the URL.
part_a.mitigation:
**Description**: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" based on the neutralization of the automatic action.

**Ingredients**: Ingredient 1: Effort Asymmetry (Friction). The email client or OS system disables direct hyperlinks within messages classified as "high urgency" or from uncertified external senders. The user must physically copy and paste the URL or manually type in the destination., Ingredient 2: Social/Rule Cues. Instead of the clickable link, the system displays an explicit microcopy: "Security Policy: Deep links are disabled for security alerts. Please manually log in to your personal area to check this notification".

part_b.audit_rule: Verifies whether the system presents warnings or alert messages with a high emotional or emergency component (Visual Flaw) allowing the user an instant and direct interaction (e.g. a link or clickable button "Solve Now") without any friction or intermediate verification step at the moment of maximum stress (Timing/Context Flaw). [ ] Pass / [ ] Fail
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Email/Web): An email that communicates a health/administrative emergency (e.g. "Increase in cases in your area") and provides a direct link to take action or inform yourself instantly.
- Domain B (Mobile): A system security alert that asks the user to verify suspicious activity on the account by offering only a generic and immediate button ("Check activity"), without going through biometric authentication.
- Domain C (Enterprise): Urgent messages from the fake corporate "Human Resources Department" requesting to download attachments (e.g. "Emergency Guidelines") by clicking on a featured zip file, bypassing the intranet.
part_b.security_risk: This design triggers compulsive behavior (reassurance seeking). Faced with the discomfort of a possible threat, the user will develop the impulse to obtain quick information and reassurance. He will end up performing the physical action of blindly clicking on the link, bypassing cognitive assessments altogether.
part_b.remediation: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" of Friction + Rules. Disable direct clickability (hyperlink) for messages classified as urgent from external sources (Friction). Replace the link with static informational text accompanied by the business rule: "For security reasons, we do not provide direct links. Log in to your personal area by opening a new tab and typing the address" (Rule Cue).
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the company regularly use internal communications with urgent direct links (e.g., HR or IT communications)? This normalizes the habit of "quick clicking", nullifying the effectiveness of the defenses against phishing.

title: Habitual E-mail Checking

part_a.trigger: The system uses an identical and indiscriminate visual design (same color, shape and behavior) for all interactive links, both for routine actions and for high-risk requests (Visual Flaw) AND allows the instantaneous execution of the action (single-click) just while the user is performing high-frequency repetitive tasks, such as rapid message routing (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From the literature): An email client that displays the fraudulent link of a phishing email (e.g. "Solve the problem of your account by clicking here") with the classic blue or purple color underlined, identical in all respects to the secure links used daily, allowing immediate opening with a single click.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Social Media): A messaging app (e.g., WhatsApp or Facebook Messenger) in which links sent by compromised contacts instantly open the in-app browser with a single "tap," taking advantage of the user's compulsive habit of quickly scrolling and clicking content.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Compulsive Behavior in its variant of automated habitual automaticity. Because checking emails or messages is such a frequently repeated action, it is stored as a "mental script." The user acts in a state of automaticity (lack of conscious attention and intentionality), feeling the irrepressible urge to "clean" the inbox or react to notifications.
part_a.error: The user physically clicks on the malicious link reflexively and instantaneously (e.g. in less than 1 second) as part of a habitual muscle sequence, instead of stopping to analytically inspect (Systematic Processing) the sender's address or the destination of the URL.
part_a.mitigation:
**Description**: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" designed specifically to interrupt muscle memory (habitual pattern interruption).

**Ingredients**: Ingredient 1: Effort Asymmetry (Active Friction). When the user clicks on a link from an external or unverified sender, the system does not open the page immediately, but intercepts the click by inserting an intermediate screen (interstitial) that forces a wait of 3 seconds before the "Proceed" button becomes clickable., Ingredient 2: Social/Rule Cues. While waiting, the middle screen shows a policy text: "You are about to leave the protected environment. Automated systems cannot verify this external link. Please check the URL before proceeding."

part_b.audit_rule: Verifies whether the system uses an identical and indiscriminate visual design for routine and high-risk links/buttons (Visual Flaw) AND allows them to be executed instantaneously (single-click) during highly repetitive operations (e.g. mail/notification sorting), without introducing friction that breaks the routine (Timing/Context Flaw). [ ] Pass / [ ] Fail
part_b.violations:
