- Domain A (Email/Web): Malicious links embedded in external emails that have the exact same visual formatting (underlined blue text) as secure internal links, and can be executed with a single click without any intermediate warning.
- Domain B (Mobile/Social): Messaging apps that open external links via in-app browsers with a single immediate "tap", indulging in compulsive scrolling of the feed.
- Domain C (Enterprise): Ticketing dashboard where the agent can open attachments provided by external customers with an instant double-click, just as they do for files uploaded by colleagues.
part_b.security_risk: This interface supports compulsive and automated behaviors (Habits/Automaticity). Users will process the task without executive control, physically clicking on dangerous links in a reflexive way even before Systematic Processing can detect the deception.
part_b.remediation: Interrupt the habit pattern interruption via a Behavioral Bundle. Enter an Active Friction: when you click on an external link, intercept the command with a pop-up that forces you to wait 3 seconds before enabling the confirm button. Add a Rule Cue: Visually explain to the user that friction is for inspecting an unverified external target.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the company require employees (e.g., customer service, secretaries) to handle huge volumes of emails with tight response times? This pushes the employee to rely on impulsive muscle automatisms to survive the workload, thwarting safety.

title: Prevention of Selective-Processing Overconfidence via Sequential Task Coupling

part_a.trigger: The system scatters multiple independent technical security indicators (e.g., origin address, digital signature status, embedded link URLs) across disparate, peripheral zones of the interface (Visual Flaw) AND it presents the primary action button concurrently, allowing immediate execution without guiding the user's attention sequentially to all relevant indicators (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature - Email/Phishing): An email client shows the sender's familiar name at the top left, but the actual hyperlink destination is only visible in a tiny status bar at the bottom left when hovering, splitting attention across the screen (Wang et al., 2016).
- Example 2 (Generalization - Mobile/Banking): A mobile banking app highlights the payee's name in massive bold text at the center, but places the modified destination IBAN number in small, light-grey font at the bottom of a scrollable view.
- Example 3 (Generalization - Enterprise/DevOps): A deployment dashboard displays a large green 'Build Ready' banner prominently, while the critical warning regarding an unsigned dependency is buried in an unexpanded side-panel tab.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Overconfidence by exploiting Variability in Attention Allocation. As proven by Wang et al. (2016, pp. 766, 772; Hypothesis 2), scattered cues lead users to engage in 'selective processing,' where they lock onto confirming evidence (familiar names) and neglect disconfirming evidence in peripheral zones.
part_a.error: The user will physically click the 'Execute,' 'Transfer,' or 'Allow' button in less than a second after scanning only a single confirming visual cue, instead of physically moving their eyes to verify all scattered security indicators.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Sequential Task Coupling Bundle: 1. Effort Asymmetry (Active Friction): Disable the primary action button by default. 2. Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF): Require the user to physically interact with/checkbox each indicator sequentially; a visual progress meter fills until the action button unlocks. 3. Rule Cues: Place microcopy stating: 'Security Policy: All indicators must be individually verified.'
part_a.criticality_context: High-value financial transaction approvals, authorization of third-party code/macros, and complex phishing triage.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization’s training program rely on simplified, 'easy' scenarios?
part_a.evidence: Wang, Li, & Rao (2016, pp. 766, 772) demonstrate that high variability in attention allocation significantly increases overprecision (Hypothesis 2: β = 0.189, p < .001). They conclude that selective retrieval of evidence contributes to judgmental bias.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if multiple independent technical security indicators are scattered across peripheral zones (Visual Flaw) AND if the action button is active before the user is guided to each indicator (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_b.violations: Browser warning titles placed top-center with certificate details in collapsed bottom-left tabs; financial apps placing 'Approve' buttons immediately below the amount while hiding destination details off-screen.
part_b.security_risk: This induces Overconfidence through Selective Processing. Users will selectively process only the most salient, confirming cues and click 'Approve' with high confidence while ignoring buried disconfirming evidence.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Sequential Task Coupling Bundle. Lock the 'Approve' button (Active Friction) and introduce a step-by-step workflow (RCF) that requires the user to interact with each indicator (origin, signature, destination) before the final action is unlocked.
part_b.org_question: Does the organization's training program rely on simplified scenarios that artificially highlight malicious cues, failing to prepare users for complex attention-allocation tasks?
part_b.reference: Wang, J., Li, Y., & Rao, H. R. (2016). Overconfidence in Phishing Email Detection. Journal of the Association for Information Systems, 17(11), 759–783.

title: Prevention of Experts' Overconfidence via Temporal Friction

part_a.trigger: The system utilizes a static toggle switch, basic checkbox, or open-ended dropdown to allow privileged users to temporarily disable a critical security control or grant a global exception (Visual Flaw) AND it does so without enforcing a mandatory system-automated expiration parameter or displaying a disruptive, persistent indicator while the risky state is active (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From Literature - Endpoint Security): As documented by Rahman et al. (2024, p. 69, Table 8), an antivirus/endpoint system allows an administrator to click a 'Disable Protection' toggle to run a blocked legitimate script (Exception Handling). The system relies entirely on the admin to manually return and flip the toggle back on later.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Cloud Infrastructure): A cloud firewall console allows a network engineer to add a temporary 'Allow All (0.0.0.0/0)' rule to troubleshoot an SSH connection, using the exact same standard UI row as permanent rules, with no auto-expiry constraint.
- Example 3 (Generalization - Identity & Access): An internal dashboard allows an admin to manually elevate a user's privileges to 'Admin' for a quick ad-hoc fix, utilizing a basic dropdown menu that lacks the automated expiration features of true Just-In-Time (JIT) access systems.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers a specific subset of Overconfidence in expert users known as the Prospective Memory Illusion. High technical expertise generates an inflated, uncalibrated self-assurance in the user's own cognitive capacity (i.e., the overconfident belief that 'I am a professional doing a 5-minute task; I won't forget to turn the firewall back on'). Because they systematically overestimate their ability to remember future intentions, they treat system-enforced safety protocols as unnecessary bureaucratic hurdles and bypass them, relying instead on their flawed, overconfident memory.
part_a.error: Driven by an overestimation of their own prospective memory, the user will physically click the 'Disable/Bypass' toggle for a temporary task, subsequently abandon the session when the task is complete, and fail to physically return to the menu to re-enable the control leaving the system permanently exposed.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Cognitive Wedge Bundle that completely eliminates the system's reliance on the expert's overconfident memory. Ingredient 1: Effort Asymmetry (Time-Bound Friction). Remove the static 'on/off' toggle for security exceptions. To disable a control, the system must force the user to physically input a specific duration for the bypass (e.g., typing '30m' or selecting from a mandatory time-bound dropdown). The system must automatically revert to the secure state when the timer expires. Ingredient 2: Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF). While the exception is active, the interface must display a persistent, high-contrast countdown timer (e.g., 'Warning: Firewall Exception Active - Auto-reverting in 14:59'). Crucially, to counter the 'Fatigue' and desensitization documented by Rahman et al. (Table 5, p. 68), this banner must visually disrupt the normal workflow (e.g., pinned to the top of the viewport, physically pushing functional content down) rather than sitting passively in a notification bell.
part_a.criticality_context: Exception handling, disabling endpoint protection/antivirus, modifying firewall rules, manual privilege escalation (pseudo-JIT access).
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization measure IT and SysAdmin performance based on strictly timed metrics like 'Mean Time To Resolution' (MTTR)? Extreme time pressure amplifies cognitive overconfidence, encouraging admins to bypass strict protocols to resolve tickets faster under the false, overconfident assumption that they will easily remember to 'clean up exceptions later.'
part_a.evidence: Rahman et al. (2024, p. 69, Table 8) explicitly identify 'Exception handling' as a primary challenge leading to negative security outcomes, noting that system administrators frequently bypass controls to execute scripts but 'forget to reinforce the control,' opening attack vectors. In human factors engineering, this 'forgetting' is not a random anomaly; it is the direct psychological symptom of expert overconfidence in prospective memory. The framework contextualizes this: because experts are highly susceptible to overestimating their memory capacity, 'cognitive wedges' (like auto-expiring temporal friction) must be used to enforce environmental redesigns over mere awareness training.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system utilizes a static toggle switch, checkbox, or open-ended dropdown to allow privileged users to temporarily disable a critical security control or create an exception (Visual Flaw) AND it does so without enforcing a mandatory system-automated expiration parameter or displaying a disruptive, persistent indicator while the risky state is active (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_b.violations: Domain A (Enterprise/Endpoint): An administrative console allows IT staff to pause the antivirus or execution restrictions on a machine by right-clicking and selecting 'Suspend Protection,' relying purely on the admin's memory to turn it back on. Domain B (Cloud/Network): A cloud security group interface allows engineers to insert a temporary 'Allow All' inbound rule to troubleshoot connectivity without requiring an expiration timer, causing the rule to become a permanent vulnerability. Domain C (Identity Management): A system allows admins to manually elevate a standard user to a high-privilege role for a specific task using a basic dropdown, with no automated system to downgrade the user afterward (failing to implement true JIT access constraints).
part_b.security_risk: This interface feeds Expert Overconfidence. Highly skilled users systematically overestimate their prospective memory (the ability to remember future actions). By relying on human memory rather than system constraints, the interface allows the user to physically disable protection for a 'quick task.' Driven by overconfidence, the user will inevitably fail to re-enable it once distracted, leaving the infrastructure permanently exposed to cyberattacks.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Temporal Friction Bundle. Replace binary 'On/Off' toggles for security bypasses with Time-Bound Friction: force the admin to explicitly set a time limit (e.g., 15 minutes) before the bypass is granted, after which the system automatically reverts to the secure state. To combat user 'Fatigue' (Rahman et al., 2024), combine this with Response-Contingent Feedback by displaying a highly disruptive, persistent countdown banner globally across the UI while the exception is active.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization prioritize rapid ticket resolution metrics (like MTTR) for IT staff in a way that creates time pressure? Time pressure reliably amplifies overconfidence, incentivizing staff to take shortcuts and rely on their flawed memory to 'clean up exceptions later' when modifying firewall rules, disabling endpoint protection, or assigning manual privileges.
part_b.reference: Rahman et al. (2024) - Towards a Taxonomy of Challenges in Security Control Implementation (Table 8: Exception Handling & Table 5: Fatigue); MORPHEUS Framework: Overconfidence in Prospective Memory & Misconfigurations.

title: The extension masking in trusted communication channels

part_a.trigger: The system doesn’t show the type of the file in the file name, representing file type only through icons [Visual Flaw] AND it does so when users download or open attachments of messages coming from the company’s mail domain [Context Flaw].
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A mailing client that, by default, doesn’t show the real extension of the attachments of all mail messages coming from an address of the company’s domain; indeed, it allows to the users to open the preview of files or downloading them just relying on the graphical icon of the software that should be used to open the file in order to understand its type, but icons can be easily manipulated and so may not reflect the real extension of files.
- Example 2 (Generalization): Considering a cloud system in which a group of users share a folder, when a user upload a new file into the folder, a notification is sent to all the users that have the desktop client of the cloud service installed on their computers; the notification just present the name of the file (without its real extension), and the icon of the software that (should) be used to open it.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The Morpheus human factor triggered in this context is the misperception, because the icon associated with the file may let the user interpret the malicious file as a harmless document, given that the system doesn’t show him the extension of the attachment in its name.
part_a.error: The user will open the preview of the file or download it and open it offline just relying on the graphical icon shown [Action] instead of inspecting the details of the attachment received in the message to verify if the extension of the file really matches the icon [Safe Action].
part_a.mitigation: Implement “Active warnings”: a thick and colored border will circle the icon associated with a file so that, when an attachment has a potentially dangerous extension, it will be colored of orange/red, according to the damages that a file with this extension may cause. (Aversive Signals combined with Response-Contingent Feedback). In order to avoid clicks on dangerous attachments, when a file with a potentially dangerous extension is opened or downloaded by the user, a pop-up will explain the potential danger that a file of this kind may carry out and it will be required to the user to click on the button Confirm in the case in which he wants to continue opening or downloading the file, on Cancel otherwise. (Effort Asymmetry)
part_a.criticality_context: Downloading and opening mail attachments from internal domains, using resources found through web-browsing and manual auditing of system files.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization have a discipline program for all employees who take time to review the details of each document received and verify the sender's credibility and, consequently, are slower to complete their tasks? Does it exist a training plan to help users learning to manage the active frictions imposed by the system to avoid opening files with potentially dangerous extensions? Does this plan turn the frictions into consolidated habits for the users of the system?
part_a.evidence: The literature underlines that security controls are frequently inefficient due to default insecure configurations, and misconfiguration and confirmation bias are the most important factors involved in the threats coming from sources that appear to be trustworthy or from ambiguous interfaces. In order to reduce the probability to fall in the most common attack techniques, it has been demonstrated that active frictions are one of the best ways that can be used to make human interventions more conscious and less automated [M. R. Rahman, B. Wroblewski, M. Tamanna, I. Rahman, A. Anufryienak and L. Williams, 'Towards a Taxonomy of Challenges in Security Control Implementation']

part_b.audit_rule: The extension masking (Misperception) > Inspection Check: verify if the system hides the real extension of files or it represents the type of the files just using graphic icons; furthermore, verify if this lack of transparency happens during the downloading or the opening of the attachments of email messages coming from an email address of the company’s domain.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Web/Email): a mailing client that, for the messages coming from addresses of the company’s domain, shows the preview of the files or allows their download without visualizing the real extensions of the attachments; Domain B (Operating Systems): an operating system (like Windows) that, by default, deactivates the visualization of file extensions, so that the users can only rely on graphic icons, which can easily be manipulated; Domain C (Cloud): a cloud collaboration platform that sends the notifications related to new or modified items of a shared folder just showing the name of the file (without the real extension) and the icon of the software with which it should be opened.
part_b.security_risk: The interface induces misperception, because users may interpret malicious files as a harmless document due to the graphic icon that indicates the software with which it should be opened, but the icon has been manipulated by attackers; as a consequence, the user will open or download the attachment, by omitting the inspection of the file details.
part_b.remediation: Implement active warnings that will circle the icon that indicates the software with which an attachment with suspicious extension will be opened. It will also be introduced an active friction that forces the user to press a confirmation button to open one of the suspicious attachments of a message, in order to break the automatic process in the user’s mind; the pop-up with the button must also contain an explanation of the most dangerous risks a file with this extension can generate.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization have a discipline program for all employees who take time to review the details of each document received and verify the sender's credibility and, consequently, are slower to complete their tasks? Does it exist a training plan to help users learning to manage the active frictions imposed by the system to avoid opening files with potentially dangerous extensions? Does this plan turn the frictions into consolidated habits for the users of the system?
part_b.reference: [M. R. Rahman, B. Wroblewski, M. Tamanna, I. Rahman, A. Anufryienak and L. Williams, 'Towards a Taxonomy of Challenges in Security Control Implementation,'

title: Aligning user perception with service criticality

part_a.trigger: The system uses identical login interfaces both for routine and sensitive services [Visual Flaw] AND the transition between low-risk and high-risk services occurs without any contextual cue signalling the change in the risk level [Context Flaw].
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An expert of the FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) has the access to the system that controls the radars and all the administrative routine tasks (access to the turns of the next weeks, punch its badge, require some days off, …); since the system presents the same authentication interface for all services, he may misinterpret the level of risk associated with the radar control service, perceiving it as comparable to routine administrative tasks.
- Example 2 (Generalization): The system used by the doctors of an hospital provides several services: it allows to consult the plan of the surgical interventions they will carry out in the following days, the canteen menu, as well as the medical records of each single patient, with all data about his health status; a doctor, since these services are accessed with the same log-in interface, may interpret the access to the patient data as a routine operation, wrongly perceiving the level of risk associated with this operation.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The Morpheus human factor triggered in this context is the misperception; since the authentication procedure is the same for high-risk services and routine operations, the user may incorrectly interpret the importance of the accessed service and he may underestimate the consequences of a credential violation and perceive the security policies as unnecessary.
part_a.error: The user will use the same simple password for routine and sensitive services [Action] instead of creating and maintaining stronger credentials for critical tasks [Safe action].
part_a.mitigation: If the authentication interface for all the low-risk services can be left unchanged, some modifications must be applied to the login page of the critical services. First of all, to introduce an active friction, the system must require the user to authenticate himself in the service by using a 2FA method, so that he is actively involved into the authentication process and forced to interpret it as a non-routine service. (Friction) The system should introduce a banner to indicate that the user is logging into a service that requires a safety-critical session and a bar will show the level of risk of the service to which the user is logging in, compared to all the others provided by the system. (Response-Contingent Feedback).
part_a.criticality_context: Authentication to services used to manage sensitive and confidential data or to safety-critical operational services (for example dashboards for configuring infrastructures).
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization require employees to access both routine and sensitive services under time pressure, potentially encouraging them to treat the authentication procedures as a routine? Does the organization have some training programs for users who still have not understood the rigid privacy policies introduced in the company or also to introduce them secure credential managers?
part_a.evidence: The paper demonstrates that when a system shares identical authentication interfaces between sensitive and routine tasks, users frequently fall into a misperception of the cyber-risks believing that “nobody will target them” or that “an attack couldn’t do much damages”; this lack of distinction leads them to adopt “coping strategies”, such as using the same password for multiple services. Reusing the same password, they confirm that cues or active frictions are necessary to signal them high-security contexts to contrast their default insecure actions. [Human Factors Considerations for Passwords and Other User Identification Techniques]

part_b.audit_rule: Prevent risk misevaluation (misperception) > Inspection check: verify if the system uses the same login interface for both low-risk and sensitive services. Furthermore, check if the system provides contextual indicators of the risk level for each one of the services supplied.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Aviation): a system used for monitoring radars and execute all employee’s routine tasks has the same authentication interface for all its services, and this let the users perceive the critical services like routine tasks and reduce their attention in using secure credentials. Domain B (Hospital): an hospital digital system uses the same login interface both for routine operations (for example showing the daily canteen menu, consulting the scheduled surgical interventions of the next weeks, …) and to access to the sensitive patient medical records; since the two interfaces are not distinguishable, doctors may distort the perception of real risks of attacks on the services, violating the hospital’s policies on passwords.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces misperception because when the authentication interface is identical for routine and sensitive services, users may misperceive the real security risks for these services and this may lead them to violate secure policies defined by the company; as a result, users may use the same password for more services with different levels of risk.
part_b.remediation: It should be introduced into the authentication page for accessing safety-critical systems a 2FA mechanism, so that the effort required to access sensitive services will be greater than the routine ones; the interface should also display a banner to inform the users that they are logging into a service that requires a safety-critical session and a visual indicator that highlight the criticality of the accessed service compared to the others provided by the system.
part_b.org_question: during the management interview, ask: Does the organization require employees to access both routine and sensitive services under time pressure, potentially encouraging them to treat the authentication procedures as a routine? Does the organization have some training programs for users who still have not understood the rigid privacy policies introduced in the company or also to introduce them secure credential managers?
part_b.reference: [Human Factors Considerations for Passwords and Other User Identification Techniques]

title: Prevention of Complacency in Link Inspection

part_a.trigger: The system displays a superficial and easily falsifiable trust indicator (such as the sender's display name or HTTPS padlock icon) by hiding the real address or destination URL behind a generic text link (Visual Flaw), and it does so in a context where the user is handling a large volume of emails or routine messages (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From Literature): A corporate email client only shows the name "IT Helpdesk" to make the interface cleaner, omitting to show that the real email is a typosquatting domain (e.g. support@microsoft-update.com instead of microsoft.com). The experienced user clicks feeling confident in the display name.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Mobile): Due to limited space, a mail app on smartphones completely hides the URL on hover (hover not possible), forcing the user to rely solely on the link text ("Click here to track the package").
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Complacency. The user, especially if they are familiar with the technology, overestimates their ability to recognize threats or assumes that they are not a target. This unfounded sense of security blocks critical analysis (System 2) and leads the user to trust the most obvious and deceptive visual elements, ignoring hidden discrepancies.
part_a.error: The user will physically and impulsively click on the malicious link in less than 2 seconds, instead of performing the safe action of inspecting the real URL (e.g. doing a "hovering" action with the mouse or expanding the sender's details).
part_a.mitigation: **Description**: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" on emails coming from the outside. The system will use a Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF): when you hover over the link, an interactive high-contrast tooltip will visually break down the URL highlighting the real domain. If the domain is unknown, Active Friction will be added: by clicking on the link, the system will block the page from loading for 3 seconds showing a Rule Cue : "This link takes you out of the company network. Please verify the domain highlighted in red before proceeding."

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system displays superficial trust indicators (like a sender's display name or generic hyperlink text) while hiding the actual source email address or destination URL by default (Visual Flaw), AND it does so in a context where the user processes a high volume of routine messages (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass/Fail)
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Desktop Email): An email client renders the sender's name as "HR Department" in large, bold font, but completely hides the actual sending email address inside a collapsed "Details" dropdown menu.
- Domain B (Mobile UI): A messaging app on a smartphone displays a hyperlink simply as "Login here" and provides no mechanism (like long-press preview) to inspect the true URL before the physical tap occurs.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces Complacency, particularly among users who consider themselves tech-savvy. Overestimating their own security posture, users will bypass analytical thinking and physically click the malicious link in less than two seconds instead of verifying the hidden true destination.
part_b.remediation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle. Combine Response-Contingent Feedback (a high-contrast tooltip that visually breaks down and highlights the true domain when hovering over a link) with Active Friction (a 3-second delay popup for external links) and a Rule Cue stating: "External Domain Warning: You are leaving the corporate network. Verify the domain."
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization's communication foster complacency by making employees believe that the automated firewall/antispam catches 100% of threats, thus discouraging them from manually inspecting links?

title: Prevention of Password Transformation Complacency

part_a.trigger: The system uses static dialing rules or a password strength indicator that visually validates security (e.g. green tick) as soon as the required special character is entered (Visual/Interaction Flaw), and does so without performing any dynamic checks to verify whether the password is a simple and predictable structural transformation (e.g. adding a number at the end) compared to common patterns (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From Literature): A web service prompts you to add a number, and the user changes his standard password from "password" to "password1", a transformation that cross-site guessing algorithms guess almost immediately.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Enterprise): A company dashboard forces employees to change their password every 90 days; the system accepts the new password because the user simply incremented the last number (e.g. from "Company2023" to "Company2024").
- Example 3 (Generalization - Mobile): A financial app requires the creation of a 6-digit PIN, and the system accepts without warning the insertion of trivial sequential patterns on physical keyboards (e.g., "123456" or "qwerasdf" converted to numbers) that simulate complexity.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers Complacency. The user expresses unfounded confidence in the sufficiency of his or her minimum effort. By satisfying the rule imposed by the interface (e.g., adding a symbol), he feels a sense of complacency that nullifies the real awareness of the risk of attacks based on dictionaries and transformation rules.
part_a.error: The user will physically type in a password that is a trivial structural variation of a password already in use (e.g. adding a number at the end) instead of generating or typing a cryptographically unique and secure string.
part_a.mitigation: **Description**: Implement a "Behavioral Bundle" based on dynamic controls. The system must cross-reference the input with known transformation models or dictionaries (Response-Contingent Feedback) in real time. If it detects a lazy variation, the system will not only reject the password, but will introduce Active Friction by blocking the form for 3 seconds, accompanied by a contextual Rule Cue : "This password follows an overly predictable pattern (e.g. number at the end). For security policies, passwords must be unique and free of common patterns."

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system relies on static composition rules or meters that visually validate the password as soon as a required character is typed (Visual/Interaction Flaw), AND it does so without dynamically checking if the password is a simple, predictable transformation (e.g., adding a number at the end) of common patterns (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass/Fail)
part_b.violations:
- Domain A (Web): A registration form highlights the password strength as "Strong" simply because the user capitalized the first letter and added a "1" at the end of a dictionary word.
- Domain B (Enterprise): An Active Directory password reset prompt allows the user to satisfy the 90-day rotation policy by simply changing "Admin2023!" to "Admin2024!".
- Domain C (Mobile): A mobile app accepts a 6-digit PIN that is a direct, simple transformation of sequential keyboard strokes without triggering a warning.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces Complacency. Users will develop an unfounded belief that their minimal effort is sufficient and will physically type a predictably transformed password (e.g., appending a digit) instead of creating a truly unique credential, leaving the account highly vulnerable to cross-site guessing algorithms.
part_b.remediation: Implement Dynamic Transformation Checks. Introduce a Behavioral Bundle combining Response-Contingent Feedback (real-time checking against known transformation patterns) with Active Friction (e.g., a 3-second delay on rejection) and a Rule Cue stating explicitly: "This password follows a highly predictable pattern used by attackers. You must create a unique phrase."
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the company rely on outdated static password composition rules that encourage lazy user transformations, rather than verifying passwords against compromised lists and known hacking patterns?

title: Security Education through embedded dynamical visual cues and concrete directly applicable suggestions

part_a.trigger: The homepage App shows informative security banners or modal with general recommendations against phishing emails [Visual Flaw] AND it presents them during low-stakes moments, rather than at the specific point of interaction with a potential threat [Timing/Context Flaw].
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): Despite the presence of cues such as the discrepancy between the display name and the actual address, syntax irregularities, and malformed URLs, users with low technical knowledge fail to engage correctly in email elaboration and general warnings are not enough to protect the user.
- Example 2 (Generalization-Mail app): Mail app shows persistent banner 'Be careful with external links'.
- Example 3 (Generalization-Bank apps): Banking applications often deploy generic anti-fraud modal pop-ups immediately upon app launching. This is an anti-pattern because it provides security information in a low-stakes context and since the user is not currently performing a sensitive operation, they lack the immediate motivation to process the information and acquire the needed knowledge which facilitate email elaboration.
part_a.human_factor_exp: Generic and out-of-context warnings fail to trigger the user's functional knowledge. This leads to a Lack of Knowledge outcome because the user might have shallow awareness that frauds exist, but the UI fails to explicitly provide the specific cues to look for during an actual threat. Consequently, the user does not learn how to distinguish signal from noise and will more likely fail to engage in email elaboration, since they have no useful information about what to look for.
part_a.error: The user will dismiss the pop-up/warning in less than 1 second without having the necessary information to process the email content and will subsequently engage in reading the email without verifying the sender's domain or inspecting the link structure.
part_a.mitigation: Studies indicate that general warnings or even training are insufficient. The waning effect probably occurs because traditional education is typically detached from the specific moment a user must make a critical decision. Nudges consisting of short and directly applicable information provided at the right time demonstrate higher efficacy. Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF). Security tools provide dynamic feedback during email interaction by integrating features like a suspicion score, which visually updates or changes color based on the specific content of the email to reflect real-time risk levels. Effort Asymmetry (Friction). The system displays the history of previous interactions with a sender, including date, time and subject line, or, if no history exists, prompts the user to verify if the communication was expected while providing a direct link for external verification on Google. Furthermore, classifying emails by their underlying intent before they are opened is useful since the user tends to focus on the content. Social/Rule Cues. The system displays alerts such as “Five colleagues have reported this email as suspicious” or by providing "check" buttons that allow users to review IT security heuristics and view a technical dissection of URLs in the emails.
part_a.criticality_context: configurations, password hygiene, phishing detection
part_a.organizational_link: “Are there any behaviors among peers that make colleagues underestimate or ignore good security habits?” “Does the company provide security training that uses gamification and realistic emails to help form better habits?” “Is there a lot of pressure to respond to emails quickly? Are "urgent" priorities often used even when they aren't necessary?” “Does the company officially adopt specific security tools for emails?”
part_a.evidence: Studies cited in the framework MORPHEUS show how email and web knowledge and experience directly influence cognitive processing and phishing susceptibility, not just because being aware of specific cues to look for increases the engagement in email-elaboration (a deep processing of message content), but also because it changes the psychological attitude (Bias), making the user more distrustful. Informational nudging has been proven to be effective only when consisting of brief embedded messages that can be immediately applied to check the email or that leverage existent users' behaviors. Also, the studies showed that the user tends not to inspect security design cues, only registering the warning color, and that the primary focus is on the email content. Zheng, Sarah Y., and Ingolf Becker. "Checking, Nudging or Scoring? Evaluating E-mail User Security Tools.". Zheng, Sarah Y., and Ingolf Becker. "Checking, Nudging or Scoring? Evaluating E-mail User Security Tools."

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the homepage presents generic, non-specific security warnings (e.g., 'Be careful with external links') without indicating concrete cues to inspect. Furthermore, verify if these warnings are shown outside the critical decision-making moment rather than being embedded directly within the user's interaction with a potentially malicious email. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A: Email app shows a permanent banner "Be careful with external links". Domain B: The system asks a user to "Check existing emails from this sender" but doesn't show directly the list of previous interactions and the user must leave the email and manually search the history
part_b.security_risk: This interface assumes prior user expertise and fails to provide actionable knowledge at the moment of need. Users remain unable to identify concrete phishing cues and will process emails superficially, leading to uninformed and potentially dangerous decisions.
part_b.remediation: Implement Just-in-Time Security Nudges. Adopt Security tools that provides dynamic feedback during email interaction by integrating features like a suspicion score, which visually updates or changes color based on the specific content of the email to reflect real-time risk levels. Show a non-blocking window about history of previous interactions with a sender, including date, time and subject line, or, if no history exists, prompts the user to verify if the communication was expected, providing a direct link for external verification on Google.
part_b.org_question: “Are there any behaviors among peers that make colleagues underestimate or ignore good security habits?” “Does the company provide security training that uses gamification and realistic emails to help form better habits?” “Is there a lot of pressure to respond to emails quickly? Are "urgent" priorities often used even when they aren't necessary?” “Does the company officially adopt specific security tools for emails?”
part_b.reference: How personal characteristics impact phishing susceptibility: The mediating role of mail processing; Checking, nudging or scoring? Evaluating e-mail user security tools

title: Informed password selection and friction

part_a.trigger: The authentication page provides only static password requirements without explaining why a password is weak or providing actionable guidance based on the user's input (Visual Flaw) AND it fails to provide meaningful feedback during password creation that helps the user understand how to improve their password (Timing/Context Flaw)
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): Corporate portals suggest general rules like using at least 8 characters or a number. These systems fail to provide specific heuristics during the selection, leading to passwords that are still very weak even if they satisfy portal requests.
- Example 2 (Generalization-Mobile): Applications, despite showing a metric for password strength, allow the selection of a weak password without warning about the use of common patterns.
part_a.human_factor_exp: Generic recommendations about password strength reinforce the Lack of Knowledge human factor by creating an illusion of competence. Users believe that satisfying basic requirements (e.g., symbols, length) is sufficient, without understanding underlying risks such as predictability or reuse.
part_a.error: The user will keep selecting weak passwords or the same password for different accounts, ignoring the risk.
part_a.mitigation: Response-Contingent Feedback (RCF). The system provides interactive messages based on the user input to guide him in building a password that is actually strong (eg. warning against common patterns of showing a crack-time).Effort Asymmetry (Friction). If a user tries to proceed with a weak password, a pop-up appears, forcing a choice: the user can either go back to strengthen the password or explicitly accept the risk after reading about potential consequences, such as identity theft or financial fraud.
part_a.criticality_context: configurations, password hygiene, phishing detection.
part_a.organizational_link: “Does the company officially provide and support the use of MFA and professional Password Managers?” “Is there a clear protocol for resetting passwords that includes protection against phishing and IT assistance?” “Are there dedicated security figures or helpdesk services available to assist users with security issues at all times?” “Do employees actually trust the security measures taken by the company, or do they perceive them as operational delays that hinder their work?”
part_a.evidence: Studies cited in the MORPHEUS framework demonstrate that a user's specific knowledge and experience and general higher education is correlated to the selection of stronger password and the use of 2FA. Many users falsely believe that only privileged accounts or administrators are targeted by hackers, which leads them to be significantly more careless with their own personal passwords. Finally, evidence shows a significant lack of trust in security tools, as many users avoid password managers because they do not fully understand the underlying technology or do not believe they are truly safe, leading to the dangerous habit of reusing the same password across multiple different sites. Nevertheless, in the study Prospects for Improving Password Selection results showed that only negative framing with specific suggestions was significantly effective in nudging the user to strengthen the password. In general, the colored metrics and the provided heuristic were not effective in building functional knowledge. Indeed, as soon as the users were presented with a site without the colored metric or suggestions, they went back to choosing weak passwords. Finally, the research suggests accepting strong passwords as default and giving concrete suggestions, but ethical implications about mnemonic effort should also be taken into consideration. M. R. Ngandu, G. Mwansa, and Z. Mkabe, "Strengthening cybersecurity in a government department by addressing password management challenges and human factor vulnerabilities" J. Amador et al., "Prospects for Improving Password Selection".

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the authentication page relies only on static password requirements (e.g., length, symbols). Furthermore, verify if the system does not provide contextual and actionable feedback during password creation to help the user improve their password. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A: A registration form accepts passwords as strong ones based only on length and symbols, without warning about common patterns. Domain B: The app shows a color-based strength meter (red/green) without explaining why the password is weak (eg., password commonly used, dates, common symbols replacement) or how to improve it. Domain C (Enterprise): A corporate system enforces complex rules but provides no feedback beyond 'Password does not meet requirements'.
part_b.security_risk: Users are likely to believe their passwords are secure when they actually follow predictable patterns. Without specific guidance, users prioritize speed over security, leading to poor password hygiene and increased vulnerability to credential-stuffing attacks.
part_b.remediation: Implement an interactive meter that updates in real-time, including a "time-to-crack" estimate or a warning if the password contains from password data breaches or dates. Replace long, static lists of requirements with adaptive hints that appear only when a specific rule is violated (date, common pattern, common replacement). When a weak password is detected, present a choice that highlights the loss. For example: "Do you want to go back and strengthen your password, or do you want to accept the risk of identity theft and financial fraud?"
part_b.org_question: “Does the company officially provide and support the use of MFA and professional Password Managers?” “Is there a clear protocol for resetting passwords that includes protection against phishing and IT assistance?” “Are there dedicated security figures or helpdesk services available to assist users with security issues at all times?”
part_b.reference: Strengthening cybersecurity in a government department by addressing password management challenges and human factor vulnerabilities; Prospects for Improving Password Selection

title: Stress Management in Critical Environments

part_a.trigger: The system uses blocking warning messages (modal dialogs) that interrupt the data entry workflow (Visual Flaw) AND imposes an immediate security decision during peak workload periods, preventing the user from completing their primary action (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): During the WannaCry ransomware attack, healthcare personnel dealt with blocked system interfaces or complex technical messages while operating in emergency situations, leading to rushed decisions in an attempt to restore care continuity.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A user utilizes an online trading app on a smartphone to execute a quick sale during high market volatility (stress and time pressure). While focused on charts, the app shows a standard pop-up for contact access; due to overload, the user does not process the permission's content and physically clicks 'Allow' instantaneously just to remove the visual obstacle.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design activates Stress and saturates Cognitive Load. Stress acts as a short-term cognitive factor that degrades the ability to make the correct choice.
part_a.error: The user performs a compulsive physical click on the close/confirm button ('OK' or 'Accept') in less than a second. This mechanical 'task-escape' serves to remove the visual obstacle to return to the clinical activity, ignoring the potential malicious nature of the prompt.
part_a.mitigation: Ingredient 1 (Response-Contingent Feedback): Insert a 'Postpone for 10 minutes (Clinical Emergency)' button that moves the notification but maintains a secure read-only mode. | Ingredient 2 (Effort Asymmetry): The actual confirmation button appears with a 3-second delay, forcing a shift to System 2 (analytical thinking).
part_a.criticality_context: Access to Electronic Health Records (EHR), management of connected medical devices.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization monitor the correlation between excessive work shifts and security incidents? Do productivity metrics penalize or discourage those who dedicate time to analyzing system warnings?
part_a.evidence: The paper by Nifakos et al. (2021) highlights that high workload and stress are cognitive factors that significantly increase phishing susceptibility and prevent accurate decisions. Reduced vigilance due to workload is identified as a primary cause of high click rates.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system presents blocking warnings that interrupt the clinical data entry flow or if it imposes critical security decisions during peak work activity. Verify that the completion of primary patient care actions is not hindered.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Healthcare): EHR software that requires full re-authentication or acceptance of new privacy policies while viewing emergency test results. | Domain B (Office/Multitasking): A corporate email client that presents a critical security warning using the exact same visual format as a routine calendar reminder, leading the user to close it mechanically. | Domain C (Cyber-Emergency): A dashboard that saturates the operator's screen with hundreds of non-priority technical logs during a critical incident.
part_b.security_risk: The interface saturates the user's cognitive resources. Stress and high workload lead to 'task-escape': the user will click 'Accept' in the face of any threat just to resume clinical activity, without analytical risk analysis.
part_b.remediation: Simplify security workflows. Implement the 'Postpone for Emergency' option and use artificial delays (3 seconds) on confirmation buttons to force the user's attention only onto threats that truly require manual intervention.
part_b.org_question: Does the company analyze whether excessive personnel workloads coincide with an increase in security violations?
part_b.reference: [Nifakos et al., 2021] (Influence of human factors on health cyber security: stress and cognitive load).

title: Mitigation of Situational Vulnerability induced by Stress

part_a.trigger: The system presents urgent security notifications using elements such as countdown timers, persistent alerts, or high-contrast warning messages (Visual Defect) AND requires immediate action without allowing delays or verification while the user is engaged in an ongoing primary activity or multitasking interaction (Timing/Context Defect).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An employee receives an urgent phishing email ('Your account will be locked immediately') during a work deadline. Situational stress reduces the ability to identify suspicious cues, leading to an impulsive response.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A smartphone mail interface showing a red banner with a countdown to 'verify the account'. The user, engaged in multitasking or task-switching (Stage 2: Access Method), clicks impulsively to eliminate the anxiety-inducing stimulus.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design exploits Stress as an internal variable of the Situational State (Stage 2). Stress suppresses the activation of System 2 (analytical reasoning) and forces the use of System 1 (fast intuitions), making the user unable to process danger signals.
part_a.error: The user performs a compulsive physical click on the malicious link or enters credentials without any verification. This 'task-escape' bypasses the critical analysis phase to resolve the problem as soon as possible.
part_a.mitigation: Ingredient 1 (Effort Asymmetry/Friction): Mandatory delay (e.g., 3 seconds) before the action.| Ingredient 2 (Response-Contingent Feedback): Dynamic feedback ('Verifying request...') during the wait. | Ingredient 3 (Rule Cue): Microcopy warning that urgent requests might be fraudulent.
part_a.criticality_context: Corporate email management during high workload, system notifications on mobile devices during multitasking.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization implement email management policies (e.g., load buffering) to protect employees? Is there a culture that allows slowing down for security checks?
part_a.evidence: The Phishing Susceptibility Model (PSM) by Zhuo et al. (2023) identifies stress and mental fatigue as situational variables that impact susceptibility by suppressing systematic processing.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system exposes the user to critical security decisions in contexts of high situational stress or time pressure. Ensure the design does not use elements (timers, persistent sounds) that exacerbate urgency.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Smart Working): Mandatory complex 'Access Review' sent on Friday afternoon exploiting fatigue.| Domain B (Mobile): Security warnings as small pop-ups while the user is in motion (GPS detected). | Domain C (Administrative): Unprioritized phishing alerts during seasonal peaks like Black Friday.
part_b.security_risk: The interface ignores the user's situational stage (Stage 2 PSM). Environmental stress leads to the abandonment of analytical reasoning (System 2) in favor of intuitive reasoning (System 1).
part_b.remediation: Implement adaptive interventions. Use effort asymmetry (forced delay) combined with dynamic feedback and warning micro-copy (Rule Cues) to force cognitive interruption.
part_b.org_question: Does the company analyze whether excessive workloads or high-stress periods for staff coincide with an increase in clicks on suspicious emails?
part_b.reference: [Zhuo et al., 2023] (SoK: Human-centered Phishing Susceptibility).

title: Managing frustration in authentication policies

part_a.trigger: The system imposes complex and restrictive password requirements (Visual Flaw) and requires mandatory password changes during primary tasks, interrupting the user's workflow (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A company system requires users to change their passwords every 30 days while they're performing work tasks. New passwords must meet complex constraints (capitalization, symbols, no reuse), blocking access until they're complete, causing disruption and frustration.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Education): A student attempts to access a university portal to take an online exam, but the system requires an immediate password change with complex and unclear rules, preventing access until the process is completed under time pressure.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design generates frustration because the user is forced to interrupt their primary task and repeatedly satisfy complex requirements. The combination of task interruption and high cognitive effort increases mental fatigue and reduces tolerance for safety procedures, encouraging avoidance and simplification behaviors.
part_a.error: The user physically reuses the same password (or a predictable variant) across multiple services or writes it down externally, rather than securely creating and managing a unique, compliant password.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle combining Response-Contingent Feedback, Effort Asymmetry, and Social/Rule Cues. The system should provide real-time password strength feedback and guidance during creation, introduce friction when users attempt to reuse previous passwords (e.g., explicit blocking or confirmation), and display microcopy explaining the rule (e.g., 'Passwords must be unique to prevent unauthorized access').
part_a.criticality_context: Access to sensitive systems such as corporate accounts, financial services, healthcare platforms, or administrative panels.
part_a.organizational_link: Does your organization impose time constraints or productivity metrics that discourage users from spending time on secure password management, encouraging the use of insecure shortcuts?
part_a.evidence: Empirical studies on password policies demonstrate that complex and frequent requirements generate frustration and cognitive load, leading users to adopt insecure strategies such as reuse, predictable changes, or externally annotating credentials.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system enforces complex password requirements and requires mandatory password changes during the execution of primary tasks, interrupting the user’s workflow (Visual + Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Enterprise): A system forces password change while the user is working on documents or emails, blocking all actions until completion. | Domain B (Education): A university portal requires immediate password change before accessing an online exam under time pressure. | Domain C (Digital Services): A banking platform blocks access until the user creates a new password with strict requirements without adequate feedback or support.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces frustration and cognitive fatigue. As a result, users adopt insecure behaviors such as password reuse, predictable variations, or external storage of credentials, increasing the risk of unauthorized access.
part_b.remediation: Redesign the password management process by introducing real-time feedback (e.g., strength indicators and suggestions), reducing task interruption, and adding friction to prevent password reuse. Combine these with clear microcopy explaining the security rationale.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization impose time constraints or productivity metrics that discourage users from securely managing passwords?
part_b.reference: Inglesant & Sasse (2010) - The True Cost of Unusable Password Policies: Password Use in the Wild

title: Preventing bypass of security controls

part_a.trigger: The system makes critical security controls optional (Visual Flaw) and allows users to skip them without any friction or verification, favoring rapid task completion over security (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): During the configuration of an enterprise Wi-Fi network, the system presents certificate verification as optional. Users can skip the check and connect quickly without any barrier, choosing the fastest but insecure option.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A mobile app requests access to sensitive permissions (e.g., location or microphone) and presents an immediate 'Allow' button, while advanced settings are hidden. The user grants access without reviewing the security implications.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design generates frustration because it exposes the user to unclear technical options without explicit guidance, making the secure path more complex and effortful. The increase in cognitive effort and decision uncertainty leads the user to reduce effort by choosing the fastest solution.
part_a.error: The user physically skips or bypasses security controls (e.g., certificate verification or permission review), selecting the fastest option instead of securely configuring the settings.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle combining Effort Asymmetry, Response-Contingent Feedback, and Social/Rule Cues. The system should introduce friction for risky actions (e.g., mandatory confirmation or a short delay before proceeding), provide real-time explanations of available options to reduce uncertainty, and display microcopy explaining the rule (e.g., 'Security checks protect your device. Avoid skipping them.').
part_a.criticality_context: System configuration, network connections, software installation, and permission management.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization provide adequate training and clear policies on security controls, or does it implicitly encourage execution speed at the expense of secure configuration?
part_a.evidence: Empirical studies on user behavior in configuration tasks show that when secure options require greater effort or are unclear, users tend to choose faster and less secure paths, bypassing critical controls.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system makes critical security controls optional and allows users to skip them without any friction or verification. Ensure that the secure path is not more complex or less accessible than the insecure one. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Networks): During enterprise Wi-Fi configuration, the user can skip certificate verification and connect immediately. | Domain B (Mobile): An app requests access to sensitive permissions by showing an immediate 'Allow' button, while security options are hidden. | Domain C (Software Installation): A system allows software installation without verifying certificates or digital signatures, offering a quick option to continue.
part_b.security_risk: The interface encourages impulsive and speed-oriented behaviors. Users bypass security controls to reduce effort, exposing the system to vulnerabilities, man-in-the-middle attacks, and unauthorized access.
part_b.remediation: Implement secure-by-default flows by introducing friction in risky actions (e.g., mandatory confirmation or delays) and providing real-time feedback and guidance. Use explanatory microcopy to clarify the importance of security controls.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization implicitly encourage execution speed over secure configuration, or does it provide adequate training on security controls?
part_b.reference: Hasan et al. (2025) - SeQR: A User-Friendly and Secure-by-Design Configurator for Enterprise Wi-Fi

title: Prevention of Security Errors Caused by Stress

part_a.trigger: The system presents a security decision using urgency cues (e.g., countdowns, 'immediate action required' messages) AND requires the user to decide while engaged in another primary task.
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): Phishing emails that create urgency significantly increase error rates, especially under stress and cognitive load.
- Example 2 (Generalization – Enterprise): A security dashboard displays 'CRITICAL: Apply patch NOW' while the administrator is handling multiple alerts simultaneously.
- Example 3 (Generalization – Mobile): A banking app requires immediate confirmation of a suspicious login with a countdown while the user is distracted or on the move.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This trigger activates Stress and Cognitive Fatigue. Stress reduces available cognitive resources and shifts decision-making from System 2 (analytical thinking) to System 1 (automatic thinking).
part_a.error: The user will physically click 'Confirm/Allow' or a phishing link immediately instead of verifying the sender or checking the URL.
part_a.mitigation: The system should implement a behavioral nudging bundle: Effort Asymmetry (introduce a mandatory delay or additional step), Response-Contingent Feedback (a dynamic indicator shows risk level and the warning disappears only after verification), and Rule Cues (e.g., 'Company policy requires verification before approving urgent requests').
part_a.criticality_context: Email (phishing), financial transactions, security alerts.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization use productivity metrics or response-time expectations that pressure users into making rapid decisions?
part_a.evidence: Stress increases susceptibility to phishing, and message characteristics such as urgency significantly influence user behavior.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system uses urgency cues AND requires decisions while the user is engaged in other tasks.
part_b.violations: Urgent phishing emails; countdown-based confirmations; enterprise alerts requiring immediate action.
part_b.security_risk: Stress leads to impulsive decisions: users approve malicious actions without verification.
part_b.remediation: Introduce dynamic feedback, friction, and explicit rule cues to slow down and guide user decision-making.
part_b.org_question: Does the organization prioritize speed over security in user decision-making?
part_b.reference: MORPHEUS; Moody et al., 2017

title: Prevention of Warning Blindness Caused by Habituation

part_a.trigger: The system uses the same visual design for frequent low-risk notifications AND presents critical warnings without interrupting the user's workflow.
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): Repeated exposure to similar warnings reduces cognitive response and leads users to ignore them.
- Example 2 (Generalization – Web): Cookie banners and security warnings use identical designs, leading users to always click 'Accept'.
- Example 3 (Generalization – Enterprise): A dashboard displays critical alerts in the same format as routine logs.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This trigger activates Habituation, which is the progressive reduction of attention toward repeated stimuli.
part_a.error: The user will physically click 'Accept/Allow' automatically without reading the warning instead of analyzing it.
part_a.mitigation: The system should implement a behavioral bundle: Aversive Signals (visually distinct high-risk warnings), Response-Contingent Feedback (the warning disappears only after active interaction), and Effort Asymmetry (e.g., requiring the user to type 'CONFIRM' for risky actions).
part_a.criticality_context: Browser warnings (downloads), app permissions, security alerts.
part_a.organizational_link: Do employees receive too many low-relevance alerts that reduce attention to critical ones?
part_a.evidence: Repeated exposure to similar warnings reduces cognitive response and increases automatic behavior (habituation).

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if critical warnings share the same design as routine notifications AND do not interrupt the workflow.
part_b.violations: Identical design for cookie banners and security warnings; uniform notifications; passive alerts without emphasis.
part_b.security_risk: Users develop warning blindness and automatically ignore or accept critical alerts.
part_b.remediation: Use visual contrast, active interruption, and required interaction to break habituation.
part_b.org_question: Is there an overload of alerts that leads to user desensitization?
part_b.reference: MORPHEUS; Moody et al., 2017

title: Prevent Automatic Response to Contextual Phishing leading to Shame

part_a.trigger: The system presents contextually relevant and highly realistic messages that closely resemble legitimate organizational communication (Visual Flaw) AND delivers these messages during routine work tasks without interrupting the workflow or prompting critical evaluation (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): In the in-situ spear-phishing study, participants received contextually relevant emails during their normal work activities. Because the messages were integrated into their workflow, users often responded without performing careful verification.
- Example 2 (Generalization – Mobile): A mobile work application sends a contextually relevant notification during an ongoing task, resembling a legitimate system request, leading the user to respond quickly without verifying its authenticity.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This trigger activates shame, as users interpret falling for a contextually relevant phishing message as a personal failure. Because the message appears legitimate and work-related, users may blame themselves for not recognizing the threat. This leads to withdrawal, avoidance, and reluctance to engage with or report the incident.
part_a.error: The user will physically click on the malicious link or respond to the email by providing sensitive information instead of verifying the legitimacy of the message. Following this interaction, the user may avoid reporting the incident instead of disclosing it through the appropriate security channel.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle combining Aversive Signals and Response-Contingent Feedback. Use high-contrast warnings to interrupt automatic behavior when interacting with suspicious messages, and provide dynamic feedback highlighting risk indicators (e.g., sender anomalies, unusual requests). Ensure that warnings persist until the user performs a safe action such as verification or reporting.
part_a.criticality_context: Email communication systems in corporate environments, credential submission processes (e.g., login requests or password updates), and situations involving urgent or time-sensitive requests requiring immediate action without verification.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization promote a culture that allows employees to report suspicious emails without fear of blame or embarrassment, or do workplace expectations discourage disclosure of potential mistakes?
part_a.evidence: Empirical findings from 'The Influence of Context on Response to Spear-Phishing Attacks: An In-Situ Deception Study' show that contextually relevant and realistic phishing messages significantly increase user interaction, especially during routine tasks. These automatic responses may lead to errors and, subsequently, shame-driven avoidance behaviors such as not reporting incidents.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system presents contextually relevant messages that closely resemble legitimate organizational communication (Visual Flaw) AND delivers them during routine work tasks without interrupting the workflow or prompting critical evaluation (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Email/Enterprise): Employees receive emails that appear to come from internal departments (e.g., HR or IT) and are aligned with ongoing work tasks, prompting immediate action without verification. | Domain B (Collaboration Tools): A message received via platforms like Teams or Slack mimics a legitimate colleague request related to current work, encouraging quick interaction without critical assessment. | Domain C (Cloud Collaboration Platforms): A user receives a notification that a colleague has shared a document related to an ongoing task (e.g., 'Updated Project Plan'), prompting interaction without verification.
part_b.security_risk: This interface exploits contextual relevance, leading users to respond automatically without critical evaluation. After interacting with malicious content, users may perceive the mistake as a personal failure, activating shame and resulting in avoidance behaviors such as not reporting the incident, increasing organizational risk.
part_b.remediation: Introduce contextual disruption mechanisms through a Behavioral Bundle. Use Aversive Signals (high-contrast warnings) to interrupt automatic responses and Response-Contingent Feedback to highlight risk indicators dynamically. Ensure warnings persist until users perform safe actions such as verification or reporting.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization encourage employees to report phishing attempts without fear of blame, or do workplace pressures discourage disclosure after mistakes?
part_b.reference: The Influence of Context on Response to Spear-Phishing Attacks: An In-Situ Deception Study

title: Prevent Incident Non-Reporting due to Shame

part_a.trigger: The system explicitly identifies individual users responsible for security incidents through visible notifications or dashboards (Visual Flaw) and presents this information immediately after the incident, making it visible to managers or colleagues (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): After a phishing incident, a company-wide email states that a specific employee caused the breach by clicking a malicious link.
- Example 2 (Generalization): After triggering a malware alert, the system displays a message stating that the user caused the security incident.
- Example 3 (Generalization): A security dashboard displays a leaderboard ranking employees based on failed phishing simulations.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design activates Shame, an emotional response that occurs when individuals feel personally responsible for a failure and fear negative judgment from others. Public exposure of mistakes makes users feel embarrassed or incompetent, leading them to avoid reporting incidents or seeking help.
part_a.error: The user physically avoids clicking the 'Report Incident' option or submitting the report, continuing their activity without notifying the security team.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle combining Response-Contingent Feedback, Effort Asymmetry, and Social/Rule Cues. Provide dynamic feedback during reporting (e.g., progress indicators), make reporting the easiest action (single-click), introduce friction for dismissing alerts (e.g., delay or confirmation step), and display a rule such as 'Reporting incidents helps protect everyone.'
part_a.criticality_context: Security incident reporting processes, including phishing reporting, malware alerts, suspicious file detection, and internal security monitoring systems.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization promote a blame-free culture that encourages employees to report incidents without fear of embarrassment or punishment, or do workplace practices discourage disclosure?
part_a.evidence: The MORPHEUS framework identifies shame as a key affective factor in cybersecurity. Studies show that users experiencing shame after a security incident tend to withdraw, avoid communication, and conceal their mistakes, reducing incident reporting and increasing organizational risk.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the system explicitly identifies individual users responsible for security incidents through visible notifications or dashboards (Visual Flaw) AND presents this information in a publicly visible context immediately after the incident (Timing/Context Flaw). (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Collaboration Tools): After a phishing incident, an automated message is posted in a shared team channel identifying the employee responsible. | Domain B (Training Platforms): A security awareness platform publicly displays a leaderboard ranking employees based on phishing simulation failures. | Domain C (Helpdesk Systems): A ticketing system labels incidents as 'user-caused error' and makes them visible across departments.
part_b.security_risk: This interface induces shame and fear of judgment. Users avoid reporting incidents or seeking help, leading to hidden security events, delayed response, and increased organizational vulnerability.
part_b.remediation: Redesign the system to remove blame-oriented feedback and prevent public exposure of individual mistakes. Implement a Behavioral Bundle: enable easy one-click reporting, introduce friction for dismissing alerts, provide dynamic feedback during reporting, and reinforce a blame-free policy through clear messaging.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Does the organization promote a blame-free culture that encourages incident reporting, or does it create fear of judgment that discourages disclosure?
part_b.reference: Shame in Cyber Security: Effective Behavior Modification Tool or Counterproductive Foil?

title: Vigilance Preservation Against Urgency-Driven Phishing

part_a.trigger: The system emphasizes urgency-loaded cues (for example, NOW, IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED, countdown deadlines, or loss-framed warnings) in highly salient positions [Visual Flaw] AND it does not present deception indicators (sender/domain mismatch, suspicious URL, unusual request context) with equal or greater salience at the decision moment [Context Flaw].
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): A decision interface presents a high-urgency cue (immediate deadline, loss-frame, alarm signal) as the dominant element, while sender authenticity markers (domain verification, sender trust indicator, official branding check) are visually suppressed or absent; users encounter the urgent call-to-action before they can assess source legitimacy.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A mobile finance push notification says URGENT: Transaction pending. Tap now to cancel, with a prominent red action button, while destination-domain and sender verification are minimized.
- Example 3 (Generalization): A high-priority enterprise chat message requests immediate credential confirmation via link, but the UI does not foreground external-domain risk markers before click-through.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The human factor triggered in this context is reduced vigilance, because urgency-driven attentional capture moves the user from deliberate evaluation to rapid heuristic responding, lowering cognitive elaboration on authenticity cues and increasing susceptibility to deception.
part_a.error: The user will click the embedded link or confirm the requested action within seconds [Action] instead of verifying sender identity, checking URL/domain legitimacy, or using an official trusted channel [Safe Action].
part_a.mitigation: Implement a vigilance-enforcing nudge bundle: introduce Effort Asymmetry with a short active delay (for example, 3 seconds) before navigation for risky links; during the delay provide Response-Contingent Feedback about sender-domain mismatch, URL reputation, and impersonation signals; add a concise policy reminder near the action control (for example, Company policy: verify external identity before credential actions).
part_a.criticality_context: Most critical during credential resets, payroll/account updates, wire-transfer approvals, and cloud document re-authentication flows, especially under time pressure or high workload.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization implicitly penalize employees who delay urgent digital responses in order to verify legitimacy, thereby incentivizing speed over verification? Is there a training plan that reinforces deliberate checks when urgency cues are present?
part_a.evidence: The literature shows that attention to visceral triggers such as urgency cues increases phishing response likelihood, while attention to deception indicators decreases it [J. Wang, T. Herath, R. Chen, A. Vishwanath, H. R. Rao, 'Phishing Susceptibility: An Investigation Into the Processing of a Targeted Spear Phishing Email', IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication, 2012].

part_b.audit_rule: Urgency-driven phishing (Vigilance) > Inspection Check: verify if, at urgent decision points, deception indicators (sender/domain mismatch, suspicious URL, unusual context) are at least as visible as urgency cues.
