part_b.violations: Domain A (Web/Email): urgent call-to-action is visually dominant while sender-domain mismatch appears only in secondary text; Domain B (Mobile): one tap opens the link immediately with no active pause and no risk cues; Domain C (Enterprise Messaging): credential or payment action is presented without nearby policy reminder and without visible external-domain warning.
part_b.security_risk: The interface induces urgency-first behavior and weakens vigilance, so users respond quickly without verification, increasing phishing success and credential-compromise probability.
part_b.remediation: Implement three concrete controls in the risky action flow: (1) timed friction: disable the primary button for at least 3 seconds when urgency keywords or high-risk intents are detected; (2) inline legitimacy panel (shown before click) with sender domain, real destination URL, and a red mismatch flag when display name and domain diverge; (3) forced choice dialog with two explicit options, Verify via official channel and Continue anyway, where Continue anyway requires a second confirmation click and is logged for audit.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: are employees negatively evaluated when they delay an urgent request to verify sender/domain legitimacy? Is this verification behavior explicitly rewarded and measured?
part_b.reference: [J. Wang, T. Herath, R. Chen, A. Vishwanath, H. R. Rao, 'Phishing Susceptibility: An Investigation Into the Processing of a Targeted Spear Phishing Email,' IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication, 55(4), 345-362, 2012.]

title: Sustaining Vigilance Through Active Link-Legitimacy Verification

part_a.trigger: The system presents context-relevant requests that appear operationally legitimate (for example, HR, IT, account, or internal workflow prompts) [Context Flaw] AND it allows immediate click-through without an explicit legitimacy-check step (sender authenticity and destination-link transparency) at the decision point [Interaction Flaw].
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): An interface presents a contextually plausible request (HR task, IT notice, finance confirmation, or operational workflow prompt) with a direct-action link, but provides no verification checkpoint (sender legitimacy check, domain preview, external-origin warning) before navigation or credential entry; the message resembles routine work communications and reduces the perceived need to pause and verify.
- Example 2 (Generalization): An enterprise email titled Payroll confirmation required includes a direct action link but does not surface destination-domain validation before click.
- Example 3 (Generalization): A mobile productivity notification says Document access expires today and offers a one-tap approval flow with no sender-risk cue or link preview.
part_a.human_factor_exp: The human factor triggered in this context is reduced vigilance, because contextual plausibility and routine framing favor fast, impulsive responding over reflective verification.
part_a.error: The user will open or click the embedded phishing link and proceed with the requested action [Action] instead of pausing to inspect link legitimacy, evaluate sender credibility, and consider potential negative consequences [Safe Action].
part_a.mitigation: Implement a vigilance-scaffolding bundle: add Effort Asymmetry through a short checkpoint before opening risky links (for example, 3-second hold-to-open or confirm step); provide Response-Contingent Feedback with real destination domain, external-origin warnings, and mismatch flags while the user is deciding; place concise policy microcopy near the action control (for example, Verify destination links before entering credentials).
part_a.criticality_context: Most critical in organizational contexts where messages appear highly pertinent to daily tasks (HR forms, IT account notices, collaboration invites), because contextual relevance can reduce vigilance and increase rapid compliance.
part_a.organizational_link: Do training and workflow policies require and reinforce routine vigilance behaviors (sender/link checking and consequence thinking), and are employees explicitly protected when they delay or refuse context-relevant requests due to failed legitimacy checks? Is there a formal escalation path for these cases?
part_a.evidence: The literature reports that successful phish responders show higher impulsivity, while participants with stronger security-hygiene behaviors (such as checking link legitimacy), suspicion toward suspicious messages, and reflection on negative consequences are less likely to click [F. L. Greitzer, W. Li, K. B. Laskey, J. Lee, J. Purl, 'Experimental Investigation of Technical and Human Factors Related to Phishing Susceptibility', ACM Transactions on Social Computing, 2021].

part_b.audit_rule: Legitimacy-check omission in plausible workflows (Vigilance) > Inspection Check: verify if context-relevant requests enforce a visible sender/link legitimacy check before action at the decision point.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Email Workflow): an operationally plausible request provides a direct link with no visible destination domain before click; Domain B (Mobile): one-tap approval completes the action without external-origin warning; Domain C (Internal Portal Messaging): sender/link verification is hidden in secondary menus and not visible at the decision point.
part_b.security_risk: The interface induces impulsive compliance with plausible phishing prompts, reducing reflective verification and increasing account-compromise likelihood.
part_b.remediation: Deploy a non-skippable verification step before opening context-relevant links: (1) show full destination domain and final redirect target in plain text (no truncation); (2) display an external-origin warning badge for non-corporate domains; (3) block immediate continuation until the user completes a quick check action (for example, tick I verified sender and domain); (4) if domain mismatch is detected, replace one-click open with a two-step confirm flow and provide a Report suspicious message button directly in the same dialog.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: when employees pause or refuse a context-relevant operational request because sender or link verification fails, are they explicitly protected from negative performance consequences and supported by a formal escalation path?
part_b.reference: [F. L. Greitzer, W. Li, K. B. Laskey, J. Lee, J. Purl, 'Experimental Investigation of Technical and Human Factors Related to Phishing Susceptibility,' ACM Transactions on Social Computing, 4(2), Article 8, 2021.]

title: Exploitation of Health-Related Saliency over Source Authenticity

part_a.trigger: The UI displays health-related threat cues (for example: 'Medical Alert', 'Lab Results') with high visual saliency through red banners or bolded central typography and it hides the sender's full domain address behind a generic display name or a collapsed header that requires manual expansion.
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): In the experimental setup by Abdelhamid (2020), 200 participants recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk were exposed to a healthcare-related phishing email adapted from InfoSec. The stimulus relied on health-related framing to trigger click intentions without offering visible authenticity markers, demonstrating how health-related concerns override visual vigilance.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A fitness app sends a push notification stating 'Account Suspended - Health Data Breach' in bold red, providing an immediate 'Secure Now' button but omitting the source verification badge until after the click.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design exploits high Health Concerns; the emotional arousal (fear/worry) triggers a 'heuristic processing' mode, where the user focuses on the high-saliency threat cues and ignores secondary authenticity markers.
part_a.error: The user will click the 'View Results' or 'Secure Account' button within 2 seconds (action) instead of expanding the sender details to verify the domain (safe action).
part_a.mitigation: Implement a 'Health-Vigilance Bundle': 1) Social/Rule Cues: Insert a permanent UI banner stating 'Official HR/Health alerts never ask for immediate secure login via external link'; 2) Effort Asymmetry: Disable the 'Open' button for 3 seconds when health-related keywords are detected; 3) Response-Contingent Feedback: Display a high-contrast 'Identity Verification' card next to the button that pulls the sender's real domain and flags it if it's external to the organization.
part_a.criticality_context: Most dangerous in healthcare management systems, corporate insurance portals, and patient-facing apps.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the company provide employees with a clear 'Safe Channel' to verify medical/insurance communications, or does the pressure to resolve health-related admin tasks quickly encourage impulsive clicks?
part_a.evidence: Abdelhamid (2020) demonstrates that health concerns act as a significant positive predictor of phishing susceptibility in health-related contexts (β = 0.157, p < 0.04), confirming that emotional arousal from perceived threats overrides cognitive vigilance.

part_b.audit_rule: Health Saliency vs Source Verification > Inspection Check: Verify if health-related alerts hide the sender's domain or use visual dominance (color/size) to distract from authenticity markers.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Health): A 'New Lab Result' alert uses a red blinking icon but the sender address is hidden; Domain B (Insurance): An urgent 'Policy Cancelled' banner lacks a clear 'Check Identity' tool.
part_b.security_risk: The interface triggers fear-based impulsivity, causing users to bypass security checks to address a perceived personal health threat.
part_b.remediation: Force a 3-second 'Vigilance Pause' on all health-related alerts. During this pause, the system must visually highlight the sender's domain in a contrasting color to the threat banner.
part_b.org_question: During the interview, ask: Is there a policy that penalizes employees for not responding immediately to 'urgent' HR or health-related notifications?
part_b.reference: Abdelhamid, M. (2020). 'The Role of Health Concerns in Phishing Susceptibility: Survey Design Study'. Journal of Medical Internet Research.

title: Suppression of Verification Tools for Suspicious/Anxious Users

part_a.trigger: The system presents critical security or credential prompts using generic, unbranded UI elements that resemble common web pop-ups and it lacks an integrated 'Verify via Official Portal' link, forcing the user to either click the provided link or navigate away entirely.
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): In the field experiment by Alhaddad et al. (2023), university students received a targeted spear-phishing email titled 'Covid-19 SOP update' (impersonating the University Health Center) threatening a RM500 fine for non-compliance. Without an integrated way to verify the mandate internally, anxious users clicked the embedded short-link to resolve the stress.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A mobile 'Login Expired' prompt appears suddenly. For a user with high Internet Anxiety, the lack of a 'Verify this request in settings' button increases the likelihood that they will either ignore a real update or click impulsively just to resolve the anxiety.
part_a.human_factor_exp: Internet Anxiety acts as a cognitive stressor. High anxiety levels generate cognitive overload; when the UI lacks clear internal verification tools, users engage in impulsive action ('Panic Clicking') to quickly eliminate the source of stress, rather than evaluating the threat rationally.
part_a.error: The user will close the legitimate security prompt (action) instead of completing the update, or click the suspicious link because no other verification path is visible (Action) instead of using a trusted manual channel (safe action).
part_a.mitigation: Implement a 'Suspicion-Resolution Bundle': 1) Social/Rule Cues: Add a permanent 'Official Request' badge that links to the corporate security policy; 2) Effort Asymmetry: Replace the 'Click here' link with a 'Go to Official App' button that opens the system settings directly; 3) Response-Contingent Feedback: If the user attempts to interact with or copy an external link anyway, immediately trigger a dynamic warning card explaining why the action bypasses official internal verification.
part_a.criticality_context: Critical for OS updates, password change requests, and multi-factor authentication prompts.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization train users to be suspicious but then provide interfaces that don't allow that suspicion to be verified safely?
part_a.evidence: Alhaddad et al. (2023) found that Internet Anxiety is a positive predictor of phishing susceptibility (p = 0.05). This indicates that highly anxious users are actually more likely to click malicious links (Panic Clicking) when the UI fails to provide safe, internal verification tools to resolve their anxiety.

part_b.audit_rule: Verification Path Availability > Inspection Check: Verify if the UI provides an official, internal way to resolve the request without clicking an external or provided link.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Desktop): A 'Security Alert' that only has a 'Fix Now' link; Domain B (Mobile): An update prompt that looks like a web banner and lacks 'Verify in Settings'.
part_b.security_risk: Vigilant and anxious users are forced into a 'double-bind': ignore a real threat or click a suspicious link, leading to system vulnerability or credential theft.
part_b.remediation: Never use 'Click here' links for security. Instead, provide a 'Open Security Dashboard' button that uses a deep link to the trusted internal application.
part_b.org_question: Ask: Do we measure how many users 'abandon' legitimate security tasks because they found the prompt suspicious?
part_b.reference: Alhaddad, M., Mohd, M., Qamar, F., & Imam, M. (2023). 'Study of Student Personality Trait on Spear-Phishing Susceptibility Behavior'. International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications.

title: Reducing Uncertainty Through Contextual Verification and Immediate Feedback

part_a.trigger: The system displays external emails with the exact same visual layout as internal trusted emails, allowing influence techniques (authority/urgency) to blend in (Visual Flaw) AND presents them when the user is operating under high cognitive load or strict time pressure to fulfill primary work goals (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From Literature): A spear phishing email that mimics a routine business communication, such as an unpaid invoice, targeting employees in roles that handle high volumes of external mail.
- Example 2 (Generalization - Mobile Comms): A messaging app notification appearing on a smartwatch from an unknown number claiming to be the CEO requesting an urgent wire transfer, blending perfectly with standard work alerts.
part_a.human_factor_exp: These triggers encourage 'heuristic processing'. Under cognitive busyness and uncertainty, individuals rely on simple cues (the sender's claimed authority) rather than in-depth consideration (systematic processing), overlooking authenticity anomalies.
part_a.error: The user will physically click on a malicious link or open a compromised attachment instead of opening the email headers to verify the actual sender address or using the IT reporting tool.
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle: Introduce Response-Contingent Feedback (e.g., a prominent 'External Sender' banner that requires user acknowledgment) combined with Active Friction (e.g., a 2-second delay before embedded links become clickable in unexpected external emails) and a Social/Rule Cue ('Corporate policy requires verifying unknown external senders').
part_a.criticality_context: Handling centralized inboxes, processing invoices, or responding to high-priority requests from supposed upper management.
part_a.organizational_link: Is security training evaluated merely on completion rates ('tick-box'), and does the organization fail to provide a closed-loop feedback system for reported emails, causing employees to feel their security efforts are a waste of time?
part_a.evidence: Williams, E. J., Hinds, J., & Joinson, A. N. (2018). Exploring susceptibility to phishing in the workplace. Focus groups reveal that employees are unaware of their vulnerability to influence techniques and rely on heuristic processing.

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the email interface uses visual friction (e.g., external email banners) to disrupt automatic habits AND if the organization provides a dedicated, feedback-oriented reporting system that supports users during high-pressure workflows. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Corporate Comms): An email system where internal and external messages look identical. Domain B (Security Training): Training materials that are static and purely informational without being interactive or relevant to the employee's job role.
part_b.security_risk: This environment triggers 'Heuristic Processing' and 'Automation Habituation'. Due to cognitive overload and the exploitation of workplace routines, the user acts automatically, clicking links without verifying the sender's identity.
part_b.remediation: Deploy 'Behavioral Interventions' such as clear, color-coded external email banners. Simplify the reporting process with a one-click button and ensure the IT department provides a 'closed-loop' feedback system.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Is security training evaluated based on behavioral change, and is there a formal process to ensure remote workers receive the same support for verifying emails?
part_b.reference: Williams, E. J., Hinds, J., & Joinson, A. N. (2018). Exploring susceptibility to phishing in the workplace. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 120, 1-13.

title: Prevention of Curiosity and Context-Matching Exploitation in Phishing

part_a.trigger: The interface presents a message that perfectly emulates the layout of an informal peer-to-peer communication, omitting visual risk indicators for unknown senders (Visual Flaw) AND it does so when the user is navigating an environment perceived as 'safe' or informal, such as a social platform or internal chat (Timing/Context Flaw).
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (From Literature): A Facebook message or email containing a link accompanied by text that leverages curiosity or a real-life context, such as 'The New Year's Eve party was awesome! Here are the pictures, don't share them!' [cite: 928, 931]
- Example 2 (Generalization - Enterprise Chat): A message in a corporate Slack or Microsoft Teams channel, apparently from a colleague in another department, sharing a link named 'Confidential_Bonus_List_2024', exploiting curiosity within a trusted internal environment.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This design triggers the Curiosity bias and Context-based decisional heuristics (Expectation Matching)[cite: 813]. The user relies on the heuristic 'this message fits my current situation' or is driven by a strong emotional desire (curiosity) to view exclusive content, bypassing rational risk analysis[cite: 1087].
part_a.error: The user will physically click on the suspicious link impulsively instead of contacting the supposed sender via an alternative channel to verify their identity or inspecting the URL manually[cite: 969].
part_a.mitigation: Implement a Behavioral Bundle: Introduce Active Friction (e.g., a 3-second mandatory 'interstitial warning' screen whenever a link from an unverified contact is clicked) combined with an explicit Social/Rule Cue ('Warning: corporate policy requires not opening unsolicited links from external senders')[cite: 724, 726, 727].
part_a.criticality_context: Use of social media, instant messaging apps in the workplace, or rapid processing of documents that fall within daily expectations (e.g., invoices, CVs)[cite: 1084].
part_a.organizational_link: Are internal security tests (phishing simulations) designed to educate, or do they unfairly deceive employees by exploiting personal curiosity or daily workload, risking damage to trust in corporate IT? [cite: 1091, 1093]
part_a.evidence: The experiment by Benenson et al. demonstrates that 34% of users click on suspicious links driven by curiosity, while 27% click because the message matches situational expectations[cite: 812]. The informal context of social platforms like Facebook significantly increases click rates compared to email[cite: 811, 969].

part_b.audit_rule: Verify if the interface (email, chat, or social dashboard) visually differentiates links sent by unknown/unverified contacts from those sent by trusted peers AND if it implements active friction before redirecting the user outside the platform's trusted environment. (Pass / Fail)
part_b.violations: Domain A (Social/Messaging): A corporate messaging app that formats links from external users identically to those from direct colleagues. Domain B (Web/Email): An email client that allows one-click activation of URLs from unknown senders without visual interruption.
part_b.security_risk: This interface facilitates the exploitation of Curiosity and Context Heuristics. Driven by curiosity or situational alignment, users lower their guard and physically click on links automatically, assuming the source is safe[cite: 1101].
part_b.remediation: Deploy a Behavioral Bundle based on friction: implement a 'click-delay' or a mandatory interstitial screen for links from unverified sources, accompanied by a clear Rule Cue to break automatic behavior.
part_b.org_question: During the management interview, ask: Do productivity metrics or the design of phishing simulations encourage employees to act impulsively on suspicious content, and is there adequate support for verifying ambiguous messages?
part_b.reference: Benenson, Z., Gassmann, F., & Landwirth, R. (2017). Unpacking Spear Phishing Susceptibility. Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg[cite: 806].

title: Prevention of Fear-Driven Compliance in Security Alerts

part_a.trigger: The system presents a high-salience threat alert with alarming wording, warning icons, or red visual emphasis and it places a single dominant action such as “Fix now” or “Verify now” at the exact moment of user interruption, while safer alternatives are minimized or hidden.
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): Scareware where users are shown fake pop-up warnings about virus infections, fraud, or disk corruption and are pushed to click a malicious executable or link (Abraham and Chengalur-Smith).
- Example 2 (Generalization): An enterprise cloud dashboard that displays a full-screen red message claiming that the session is compromised and offers a large “Re-authenticate now” button while hiding “View details” or “Contact IT support”.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This trigger activates fear, intended as an affective state linked to perceived immediate danger. In the MORPHEUS logic, emotional factors are central because interface conditions can trigger affective reactions that shape insecure behavior.
part_a.error: The user will physically click the urgent action button instead of verifying the legitimacy of the alert, checking the source, or choosing a safer support path.
part_a.mitigation: The interface should redesign the risky flow using a behavioral bundle: add friction before the dangerous action, provide dynamic feedback while the user is deciding, and show a clear rule cue (e.g., 'Never install security software from pop-up alerts').
part_a.criticality_context: Malware warnings, account recovery screens, browser security alerts, endpoint protection interfaces, and permission-granting tasks.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization train users to verify security alerts through official internal channels?
part_a.evidence: Abraham & Chengalur-Smith; explains that social engineering manipulates emotions such as fear through fake infection pop-ups that lead users to click malicious links or executables.

part_b.audit_rule: Check whether the system uses fear-inducing security alerts that push users toward one dominant risky action without immediate verification support. FAIL if the interface combines alarming threat framing with a dominant action button and weak visibility of safer alternatives.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Software/Web): Fake malware warnings. Domain B (Enterprise/UI): 'Fix now' as only salient option with hidden details. Domain C (OS/System): Alerts at interruption points with no verification support.
part_b.security_risk: Fear-based interfaces can trigger impulsive compliance and lead users to click malicious links, install rogue software, or disclose credentials.
part_b.remediation: Introduce a behavioral bundle combining friction, response-contingent feedback, and explicit rule cues near the decision point.

title: Reducing Fear-Based Response to Smishing Messages

part_a.trigger: The system displays a security-related SMS, push notification, or lock-screen message that implies imminent loss, account compromise, or urgent legal or administrative consequences, and it allows the user to call, tap, or reply immediately without surfacing trustworthy verification cues.
part_a.examples:
- Example 1 (Literature): Rahman et al. tested realistic SMS attacks (Facebook login/IRS lawsuit) where fear-based scenarios and action patterns (CALL/REPLY) led 16.92% of participants to respond.
- Example 2 (Generalization): A banking application that mirrors incoming SMS warnings on the lock screen and allows users to tap the link directly without first showing sender authenticity or destination verification.
part_a.human_factor_exp: This trigger activates fear by presenting the possibility of immediate damage and encouraging instant damage-control. MORPHEUS identifies fear, urgency, and trust as core mechanisms exploited in social engineering.
part_a.error: The user will physically tap the link, call the number, or reply to the message instead of opening a trusted official app, independently verifying the sender, or reporting the message.
part_a.mitigation: Behavioral bundle: Make the risky path harder by adding friction (e.g., disable direct links); provide response-contingent feedback (sender verification); and include rule cues (e.g., 'Do not verify account problems from SMS links').
part_a.criticality_context: SMS apps, banking applications, delivery or government-service notifications, identity-verification flows, and enterprise mobile authentication.
part_a.organizational_link: Does the organization train users to handle suspicious mobile messages by opening the official app or channel directly?
part_a.evidence: Rahman et al., Users Really Do Respond To Smishing; provides direct empirical evidence that users respond to realistic fear-based SMS attacks, specifically in account-loss scenarios (34.62% success rate).

part_b.audit_rule: Check whether mobile security-related messages allow immediate fear-driven compliance without presenting trustworthy verification support at the moment of choice. FAIL if the system allows direct tap/call/reply without clear sender validation.
part_b.violations: Domain A (Telecom): Threatening SMS with direct links. Domain B (Fintech): Banking warnings with mirrored notifications. Domain C (OS): Lock-screen actions that bypass verification.
part_b.security_risk: Users may respond impulsively to smishing by clicking malicious links, calling attacker-controlled numbers, or revealing account information.
part_b.remediation: Redirect users toward trusted in-app verification, add friction to direct response actions, show clear verification cues, and place explicit anti-smishing rules at the decision point.
part_b.org_question: Does the organization train users to handle suspicious mobile messages by opening the official app or channel directly?
part_b.reference: Rahman et al., Users Really Do Respond To Smishing.
